title: The Climbing Water: how a plant drinks from root to leaf

summary.text: This unit follows one drop of water through a plant. The drop goes in through tiny hairs on the roots. It climbs up the stem through tubes thinner than a hair. Then it spreads along the veins of the leaves and flowers. Most of it slips out of tiny holes in the leaves, into the air, as invisible vapour. As water leaves the top, it pulls more water up behind it. Water can do this because it sticks to itself, like a chain of hands. The Sun's warmth does the lifting, not a heart or a pump. You will turn white flowers blue and catch a plant's breath in a bag. You will also meet a great Indian scientist who argued about all this. Some parts are still a mystery, like how the tallest trees keep their water chains from snapping.
summary.art: A cut-away drawing of a tulsi plant in a pot: tiny blue drops entering root hairs, climbing a glowing tube inside the stem, spreading through the leaf veins and floating out of the leaves as faint mist towards a warm Sun.

intro.hook: Look at a tall coconut palm or a neem tree. Its top leaves are wet inside, high up in the sun. But the water is down in the soil. Nobody carries it up. There is no heart and no pump. So how does the water climb?
intro.text: Try this tonight. Mix lots of food colour into a glass of water. Stand a white flower, or a stalk of balsam or celery, in it. Go to sleep. In the morning, look at the petals and leaves. Something will have travelled up the stem while you slept. This unit is about that hidden journey. It follows water through a plant, from the root to the very top leaf.
intro.art: A white tuberose stem standing in a glass of deep blue water on a windowsill at night, and the same flower at dawn with blue-edged petals.

outcomes: I can trace the path of water through a plant: into the roots, up the stem, and out to the leaves and flowers.
I can set up the coloured-water experiment, keep it a fair test, and use what I see as evidence that a stem has tubes inside.
I can explain that leaves let water out into the air as invisible vapour, and that this pulls more water up the stem.
I can explain why a plant wilts, how to help it, and why flower sellers cut stems again under water.
I can measure how fast water climbs or is used up, and show my results in a table and a bar chart.
I can say what scientists agree on about how water climbs a tall tree, what they argued about, and what is still unknown.
I can explain the deep ideas: water molecules holding on to each other, the Sun doing the lifting, forests making rain, and thirsty plants that click.

terms.meaning: The part of a plant that grows into the soil. It holds the plant firm and soaks up water.
terms.example: Pull up a weed gently. The white threads under it are its roots.
terms.art: A small weed lifted from the soil with its white roots hanging down.

terms.meaning: A very thin, fuzzy hair on a young root. Each one is a single long cell. Root hairs push between bits of soil and soak up water.
terms.example: Sprout a moong seed on a wet cloth. The white fuzz on its root is root hairs.
terms.art: A moong sprout seen through a magnifying glass, its root covered in white fuzz.

terms.meaning: To soak something up, the way a sponge soaks up water.
terms.example: Roots absorb water from wet soil.
terms.art: A sponge corner dipped in water, the water creeping up into it.

terms.meaning: The part that holds a plant up. It carries water up from the roots to the leaves and flowers. A tree's trunk is a big, woody stem.
terms.example: The stalk of a celery or a balsam plant is its stem.
terms.art: A balsam plant with its see-through green stem highlighted.

terms.meaning: To carry something from one place to another.
terms.example: A truck transports vegetables to the market. A stem transports water to the leaves.
terms.art: A vegetable truck on a road beside a plant stem with water drops moving up it.

terms.meaning: The tiny water tubes inside a plant. They run from the roots, up the stem, and into every leaf. Most are thinner than a hair.
terms.example: The stringy threads you pull out of a celery stalk are bundles of xylem.
terms.art: A celery stalk cut across, showing a ring of coloured dots, each dot a bundle of tubes.

terms.meaning: A line you can see on a leaf or petal. Veins hold the water tubes that bring water to every part of the leaf.
terms.example: Hold a peepal leaf up to the light. The lines are its veins.
terms.art: A peepal leaf held up against the sun, its veins glowing like a map of roads.

terms.meaning: When liquid water turns into an invisible gas and floats off into the air.
terms.example: Wet clothes on a line dry because the water evaporates.
terms.art: Clothes drying on a line in the sun with faint wavy lines rising from them.

terms.meaning: Water as an invisible gas in the air. When it cools, it turns back into drops.
terms.example: A cold steel tumbler gets drops on the outside. They come from water vapour in the air.
terms.art: A cold steel tumbler with water droplets on its outside.

terms.meaning: Water leaving a plant's leaves as invisible vapour. As water leaves the top of the plant, it pulls more water up the stem.
terms.example: Tie a clear bag over a leafy branch. After an hour, the inside is misty. That is transpiration.
terms.art: A clear plastic bag tied over a leafy branch, misty and dotted with drops inside.

terms.meaning: A tiny hole in a leaf, far too small to see without a microscope. One hole is a stoma. Many are stomata. Water vapour goes out of them, and air comes in.
terms.example: Most of a mango leaf's stomata are on its underside.
terms.art: A microscope view of a leaf's underside, with many small mouth-shaped holes.

terms.meaning: Two curved cells around each leaf hole, like two lips. They open the hole or close it.
terms.example: On a very hot, dry afternoon, guard cells often close the holes so the plant loses less water.
terms.art: A close-up of one leaf hole with two bean-shaped guard cells, shown open and then closed.

terms.meaning: When a plant goes floppy and droops because it is losing water faster than it can drink.
terms.example: Coriander left out of the fridge on a hot day wilts.
terms.art: A bunch of coriander drooping over the edge of a kitchen counter.

terms.meaning: When a plant's cells are full of water, they push against each other like water balloons in a bag. That makes stems and leaves stand up stiff.
terms.example: Fresh palak leaves are crisp and firm. Old ones go limp.
terms.art: A bag packed tight with small water balloons beside a crisp spinach leaf.

terms.meaning: The tiniest bit of something that is still that thing. A water molecule is made of three atoms: two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom.
terms.example: One drop of water has more molecules than there are grains of sand on all of India's beaches.
terms.art: A water drop with a zoom circle showing tiny shapes like a small ball with two smaller balls stuck on, like Mickey Mouse ears.

terms.meaning: Water molecules sticking to each other, like people holding hands in a long chain.
terms.example: A drop of water on a leaf stays round, because its molecules hold on to each other.
terms.art: A long chain of cartoon water molecules holding hands, climbing up a thin tube.

terms.meaning: Water creeping up into very thin gaps by itself, because it sticks to the sides of the gap.
terms.example: Dip the corner of a tissue in tea. The tea climbs up the tissue.
terms.art: A tissue corner dipped in a cup of tea, the brown colour creeping upwards.

terms.meaning: A small push from the roots that squeezes water a little way up the stem, mostly at night.
terms.example: On some mornings, grass tips have tiny beads of water squeezed out of them.
terms.art: Blades of grass at dawn, each tip holding one bright bead of water.

terms.meaning: The plant's second set of tubes. They carry sugary food made in the leaves to the rest of the plant. This unit is about the water tubes, the xylem.
terms.example: Sugarcane juice is sweet because the cane stores food carried in its phloem.
terms.art: A stem cut open showing two kinds of tubes side by side, one with blue drops and one with golden sugar.

terms.meaning: A test where you change only one thing, and keep everything else the same. Then you know what caused the difference.
terms.example: Two celery stalks in the same coloured water, one with leaves and one without. Only the leaves are different.
terms.art: Two identical glasses of coloured water, one celery stalk with leaves and one with its leaves cut off.

terms.meaning: What you saw or measured that shows your idea is true, or not true.
terms.example: The blue dots inside a cut celery stalk are evidence that water climbed up tubes.
terms.art: A child pointing at a ring of blue dots in a cut celery stalk, a notebook open beside it.

explanations.concept: The path of water: root, stem, leaf, air
explanations.definition: Water enters a plant through its roots. It travels up the stem in tiny tubes. It spreads through the veins to every leaf and flower. Most of it then leaves through tiny holes in the leaves, as invisible vapour.
explanations.description: Think of a plant as a long, thin road for water, going one way. The road starts in the soil, where root hairs soak up water. It runs up through the stem, like a bundle of very fine straws. In the leaves, it splits into many small lanes: the veins. At the end of every lane are tiny holes, and the water slips out into the air. Some water stays behind, to keep the plant firm and to help the leaves make food. The unit 'Food from light: photosynthesis' tells that part of the story.
examples: Water a tulsi pot. The water goes into the roots, not the leaves.
A banana leaf's long straight veins carry water from the middle stalk to the edges.
On a hot day a neem tree sends water from deep soil to leaves higher than a house.
explanations.art: A labelled path drawn on a plant: 1 root hairs in soil, 2 tubes in the stem, 3 veins in the leaf, 4 mist leaving the leaf into the air.
explanations.context: This card gives the big picture of the whole unit: the path one drop of water takes through a plant.

explanations.concept: The tubes inside a stem: xylem
explanations.definition: Xylem is the set of tiny tubes that carry water from the roots to the leaves. They run the whole length of the plant, and into every vein.
explanations.description: A stem is not a solid stick. Inside, it is packed with bundles of tubes. Most of them are thinner than a hair. Each tube is made of cells that have died and lost their insides. Their end walls opened up, so the cells join into long hollow pipes. Think of many cups with no bottoms, stacked one on top of another. In celery, the bundles are the stringy threads you can pull out. When you stand celery in coloured water and then cut it across, each coloured dot is one bundle. In a tree, the xylem is the wood itself. Every year the tree adds a new ring of water tubes.
examples: The tough strings in a celery stalk or a stick of sugarcane are bundles of tubes.
The rings in a cut tree trunk are layers of old water tubes, one for each year.
The lines on a white rose petal fill with colour when its stem stands in coloured water.
explanations.art: A zoom in three steps: a celery stalk, its cut end with a ring of blue dots, then one dot opened up into a bundle of hollow tubes like stacked bottomless cups.
explanations.context: You cannot see water climbing inside a plant. This card explains the hidden tubes it climbs through.

explanations.definition: Transpiration is water leaving a plant through tiny holes in its leaves, called stomata, as invisible water vapour.
explanations.description: Each leaf is covered in tiny holes, far too small to see. A patch of leaf the size of your little fingernail can have thousands of them. Each hole has two curved guard cells around it, like two lips. When the holes open, air comes in. The leaf needs a gas from the air to make its food. But as the holes open, water vapour escapes too. A plant cannot have one without the other. That is why most of the water a plant takes up does not stay in it. Most of it goes back into the air.
examples: A clear bag tied over a leafy branch turns misty inside within an hour in the sun.
A potted plant covered with a clear jar in the sun gets drops on the inside of the jar.
A cactus has very few holes, and opens them mostly at night, when the air is cool.
explanations.art: A leaf seen up close with tiny mouth-shaped holes on its underside, faint wisps of vapour leaving some of them.
explanations.context: Where does the water go when it reaches the leaves? This card explains that most of it leaves through tiny holes, into the air.

explanations.definition: Water is pulled up a plant from the top. As water evaporates from the leaves, it tugs on the water behind it. Because water molecules hold on to each other, the whole thread of water in each tube moves up.
explanations.description: Imagine a long line of children holding hands, standing up a staircase. The child at the top lets go and runs off. Everyone else steps up one stair to close the gap. A new child joins at the bottom. That is how water climbs a plant. Each water tube holds one unbroken thread of water, from the roots to a leaf. When a bit of water evaporates from the leaf, the thread is pulled up a little. New water is soaked up at the roots to fill the bottom. Scientists call this the cohesion-tension idea. Cohesion means water sticking to itself. Tension means a pull, like a stretched rope.
examples: A leafy celery stalk pulls coloured water up faster than a stalk with its leaves cut off.
Trees drink most in the hot, sunny middle of the day, when their leaves lose the most water.
Drinking through a straw is a pull from the top too, but a tree pulls in a different way.
explanations.art: A line of children holding hands up a staircase inside a tree trunk. At the top, one child skips off into the air as a little cloud, and the rest step up.
explanations.context: This card explains how water climbs up a plant, all the way to the top leaf, with no pump.

explanations.concept: An old argument: push, pump or pull?
explanations.description: For three hundred years, scientists argued about how water reaches the top of a tree. Some thought the roots pushed it. Some thought living cells pumped it. Some thought the leaves pulled it. Today, almost all plant scientists agree that the pull from the leaves does most of the work. Sometimes the roots give a small push too. But the story of the argument is a great story about how science works.
examples: Cut a grapevine stem in spring and sap drips out of the stump. That drip is a push from the roots.
Coloured water still climbs up a stem whose living cells have been killed. So living pumps are not needed.

perspectives.who: Stephen Hales, an English clergyman and scientist, in his book Vegetable Staticks, 1727
perspectives.explanation: He weighed potted plants and measured how much water they lost through their leaves each day. He also fixed glass tubes to cut vine stems and saw sap pushed up the tubes. He showed that roots can push, and that leaves lose a lot of water.

perspectives.who: Eduard Strasburger, a German botanist, in 1891
perspectives.explanation: He killed the living cells in long stems with poison and heat. Coloured liquid still climbed up them. So whatever lifts the water does not need living cells along the way.

perspectives.who: Henry Dixon and John Joly, two scientists in Dublin, Ireland, in 1894
perspectives.explanation: Water is pulled up from the top. Leaves let water evaporate, and that tugs on unbroken threads of water in the tubes. Water molecules cling together so strongly that the threads do not snap. This is the idea accepted today.

perspectives.who: Jagadish Chandra Bose, an Indian scientist in Kolkata, in his book The Physiology of the Ascent of Sap, 1923
perspectives.explanation: A layer of living cells in the stem squeezes in a rhythm, like tiny hearts, and pumps the water upwards. He built clever instruments to show plants pulsing. Most scientists were not convinced, and this idea is now rejected. Bose is still honoured for showing that plants sense and respond.

explanations.art: Four small portraits in a row: Hales with a potted plant on a scale, Strasburger with a glass tube, Dixon and Joly with a tall tree diagram, Bose with his recording instrument.
explanations.context: Scientists argued for a long time about what lifts water up a tree. This card tells the story of that argument and who said what.

explanations.concept: Why plants wilt, and spring back
explanations.definition: A plant wilts when it loses water from its leaves faster than its roots can take water in. Its cells go soft, like half-empty water balloons, and the plant droops.
explanations.description: Every plant cell has a stretchy bag inside that fills with water. When all the cells are full, they press hard against each other and against their walls. That pressing makes leaves and soft stems stand up firm. When water runs short, the cells go soft and floppy. Then the stem bends and the leaves hang down. Give a wilted plant water soon, and the cells fill up again. In an hour it can stand tall. But if it stays dry too long, the cells are damaged and it may not recover.
examples: Wilted coriander stood in a glass of water perks up within an hour or two.
Garden plants often droop in the hot afternoon, then stand up again in the cool evening.
A plant pulled up roughly wilts, because its root hairs are torn off and it cannot drink.
explanations.art: Two pictures side by side: a drooping balsam plant with cells drawn as soft half-empty balloons, and the same plant upright with plump full balloons.
explanations.context: Have you seen a plant droop on a hot day? This card explains what wilting is, and why water brings a plant back.

explanations.concept: What makes a plant drink faster
explanations.definition: A plant loses water faster, and so drinks faster, when it is sunny, warm, windy and dry. It loses water more slowly when it is dark, cool, still or damp.
explanations.description: Think about drying clothes. They dry fastest on a hot, sunny, windy day, and slowest on a damp, still night. Leaves lose water in the same way. Sunlight also makes most plants open their leaf holes, to let air in for making food. More leaves mean more holes, so a leafy stem drinks faster than a bare one. The chart shows made-up results from the leafy and bare stem test in this unit.
examples: A plant on a sunny balcony needs watering more often than one in a shady room.
Desert plants like cactus have few leaves, or none, so they lose less water.
Farmers in hot places often water in the early morning or evening, when less is lost to the air.
explanations.art: Four small pictures of the same potted plant: in hot sun with a fan blowing, in shade, at night under the Moon, and on a misty damp morning, with big or small vapour arrows.
explanations.context: Some days plants drink a lot and some days hardly at all. This card explains why, using a test you can do with two stems in water.

chart.title: Made-up example: how much the water level dropped in 2 days
chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what results can look like. Your numbers will be different.

explanations.definition: Water molecules pull on each other. This is called cohesion. They also cling to the walls of thin tubes. This is called adhesion. Both come from tiny electric pulls between molecules.
explanations.description: A water molecule is one oxygen atom with two hydrogen atoms stuck on. It looks a bit like a head with two ears. The oxygen end has a tiny bit of negative electric charge. The hydrogen ends have a tiny bit of positive charge. Opposite charges pull on each other. So the hydrogen end of one molecule tugs on the oxygen end of the next. Each molecule holds a few neighbours like this, again and again, all through the water. Scientists call these hydrogen bonds. They are why a drop is round, and why a water strider can walk on a pond. They are also why a thread of water in a tree can be pulled up without snapping.
examples: A paperclip laid gently on still water can float, held up by the water's skin.
Fill a steel tumbler to the brim, then add drops one by one. The water bulges above the rim before it spills.
Water creeps up a tissue because it clings to the paper and to itself.
explanations.art: A zoom into a water drop: many small Mickey-Mouse-shaped molecules, the ear ends of each one tugging the head of the next with little dotted lines.
explanations.context: Why does a thread of water not snap as it is pulled up a tree? This card zooms in to the tiny bits that water is made of.

explanations.definition: The energy that lifts water up a plant comes from the Sun. Sunlight warms the leaves and makes water evaporate. The plant does not spend its own food energy to lift the water.
explanations.description: Lifting water is work. Ask anyone who has carried a bucket up the stairs. Your heart spends energy every second to push your blood round. A tree has no heart. Instead, sunlight warms the wet inside of each leaf, and water evaporates out of the holes. Turning water into vapour takes a lot of energy, and that energy comes from sunlight. The leaves just let the Sun do it. As a bonus, the leaves cool down, the way sweat drying on your skin cools you. That is part of why the shade of a big tree feels so cool.
examples: Sweat drying on your arm cools you. Water leaving a leaf cools the leaf.
On a hot day, the air under a big neem or banyan tree feels cooler than the air in a car park.
explanations.art: A big Sun sending golden rays into a leaf. Inside the leaf, water drops turning into vapour and flying out, and a thread of water rising up the stem below.
explanations.context: Something must do the hard work of lifting water up a tree. This card explains that the power comes from the Sun.

explanations.concept: Why a straw cannot do what a tree does
explanations.definition: When you suck on a straw, the air pushing on the drink outside pushes it up the straw. That push can only lift water about 10 metres, even with a perfect pump. Tall trees lift water much higher, so they must work in a different way.
explanations.description: Sucking does not really pull the drink. It takes air out of the straw. Then the air pressing on the drink in the glass pushes it up into the straw. But the air can only push water up about 10 metres, the height of a three-storey building. No suction pump can lift water higher than that. Yet the tallest tree alive, a coast redwood called Hyperion in California, is about 116 metres tall. Its water threads are not pushed up by air. They are pulled from the top and hang together by cohesion, like a rope being pulled up a well. Scientists say the water in a tall tree is under tension, a stretching pull.
examples: A simple suction hand pump cannot lift water from deeper than about 8 to 10 metres. Deep wells need a pump down at the water.
A coconut palm can be 25 metres tall. That is already more than twice the straw limit.
explanations.art: A side-by-side picture: a giant straw reaching 10 metres up a building, with water stopping at the 10 metre mark, next to a towering redwood with water reaching the top.
explanations.context: Is a tree like a giant drinking straw? This card shows why it cannot be, using the height limit for sucking.

explanations.concept: Bubbles in the tubes, and plants that click
explanations.description: The water threads in a tree are stretched tight. If the plant gets very thirsty, a thread can snap and a tiny air bubble can form in the tube. Scientists call this an embolism. A tube with a bubble cannot carry water. Flower sellers know about this. They cut flower stems again under water, so no air gets into the fresh tube ends. Snapping threads also make tiny clicks. In 1966 scientists John Milburn and Robert Johnson listened to thirsty castor plants with special microphones and heard the clicks. In 2023, a team in Tel Aviv, Israel, led by Lilach Hadany, recorded thirsty tomato and tobacco plants clicking. The sounds were too high for people to hear, but could be picked up from about 10 centimetres away.
examples: Cut roses last longer when their stems are trimmed under water.
A thirsty tomato plant in the Tel Aviv study clicked dozens of times an hour. A well-watered one hardly clicked at all.

perspectives.explanation: The clicks most likely come from water threads snapping and bubbles forming in thirsty tubes.
Moths, mice or other plants might be able to hear these clicks and learn that a plant is thirsty. Nobody has shown this yet.
Clicks are just a side effect, like a creaking floor. A plant is not trying to say anything. The question is still open.

explanations.art: A thirsty tomato plant in a pot with a tiny microphone near its stem, little sound waves coming out, and a magnified tube inside with an air bubble.
explanations.context: What happens when a thirsty plant's water threads snap? This card is about air bubbles in the tubes, and a recent surprise: plants that click.

explanations.description: The first plants on land were small and flat, like mosses today. They had no proper water tubes. So they had to stay low, close to damp ground, and soak water up through their whole body. Fossils show that by about 430 million years ago some small plants had simple water tubes. Later, plants used a tough material called lignin to make their tubes and stems stiff. Lignin is what makes wood hard. With strong pipes, plants could grow upwards and reach the light above their neighbours. By about 385 million years ago, the first forests of tall trees had grown. Scientists agree on this broad story from the fossils. The exact dates and order keep changing as new fossils are found.
examples: Moss on a wall in the monsoon stays only a few millimetres tall.
A fern has water tubes, and grows much taller than moss.
A banyan tree's hanging roots grow down to the soil and become new pillars that carry water too.
explanations.art: A timeline strip: flat moss on wet rock, a small stick-like early plant with a tube drawn inside, a fern, and then a tall ancient forest.
explanations.context: Why are mosses tiny and trees huge? This card is about how water tubes let plants grow tall, hundreds of millions of years ago.

explanations.description: All the water leaving leaves goes up into the air. Over a forest, it can form clouds and fall again as rain, further along. Scientists have measured this in the Amazon rainforest in South America. The forest sends so much water into the air that some call it a flying river. Plants are a big part of the water cycle. That is the endless trip of water from land and sea, up to the sky, and back. But how big a part? Scientists still argue about that.
examples: A big tree on a hot day can send hundreds of litres of water into the air.
Cutting down large forests can make the land around them drier.

perspectives.who: Scott Jasechko and colleagues, in the journal Nature, 2013
perspectives.explanation: They estimated that plants send up most of the water that rises from land: about 80 to 90 out of every 100 drops. The rest evaporates from soil, lakes and rivers.

perspectives.who: Other scientists, including William Schlesinger and Jasechko himself, in 2014
perspectives.explanation: After more studies, they gave a lower estimate: about 60 out of every 100 drops. Different methods give different answers.
Plants send a very large share of the land's water back into the sky. The exact amount is still being measured.

explanations.art: A green forest with mist rising from the treetops, forming a long cloud river that rains down on farms further away.
explanations.context: What happens to all the water that leaves leaves? This card follows it into the sky, and into an argument about how much rain plants make.

chart.title: Of 100 drops of water rising from land, how many come from plants? (one 2014 estimate)

data.label: From soil, lakes and rivers: about 40

explanations.concept: How tall can a tree grow?
explanations.description: The higher water has to climb, the harder the pull on the thread. And the harder the pull, the more likely the thread is to snap. In 2004, George Koch and his team climbed the tallest redwood trees in California and studied their top leaves. The top leaves were small and thirsty, as if the water barely reached them. From this they estimated that no redwood could grow much taller than about 122 to 130 metres. The tallest known tree, Hyperion, is about 116 metres. Other scientists think other limits, like wind and getting enough food to the top, also matter. Nobody knows for sure.
examples: The tallest kinds of tree, coast redwoods and mountain ash trees from Australia, can grow taller than 90 metres.
A redwood's top leaves are much smaller than its lower leaves.
explanations.art: A giant redwood next to a tall building for scale, with a dotted line above its top labelled 'the limit?' and a scientist on a rope near the top.
explanations.context: Could a tree grow as tall as a mountain? This card is about the limit that water sets on how tall trees can grow.

explanations.concept: Plants and bodies: a pull, not a pump
explanations.definition: Your blood is pushed round your body in a loop by your heart. A plant's water goes one way, from root to leaf, pulled from the top by evaporation. Most of the water tubes are dead cells.
explanations.description: You and a plant both need to move water to every part. Your body uses a living pump, your heart, and living pipes, your blood vessels. The blood goes round and round. A plant uses dead, hollow tubes and the pull of the Sun. The water goes one way only, up and out. A plant does have a second set of living tubes, the phloem, that carry sugary food both up and down. Both of you cool off in the same way, though. You sweat. A leaf lets water evaporate.
examples: When you run, your heart beats faster to push more blood. On a hot day, a plant pulls more water.
Blood keeps going round your body. Water in a plant leaves it, and goes into the sky.
explanations.art: Two outlines side by side: a child with a red heart and a loop of blood vessels, and a tree with blue upward arrows and mist leaving the leaves.
explanations.context: How is a plant moving water like your body moving blood? This card compares the two, and finds one big difference.

explanations.concept: Plants in space, and the water's long journey
explanations.definition: In space, water does not drip downwards. So astronauts on the International Space Station grow plants in soft pillows with wicks. The wicks feed water to the roots by capillary action.
explanations.description: On Earth, gravity pulls water down into the soil and around the roots. On the space station, everything floats. Water clumps into wobbly balls and can drown roots or float away. NASA's Veggie garden grows lettuce in small pillows of soil that soak up water through wicks, like a cotton thread. The water in your plant also has a very long story. Its hydrogen was made soon after the universe began, about 13.8 billion years ago. Its oxygen atoms were made inside stars that exploded long before the Sun was born. The same water has been through clouds, seas, dinosaurs and trees, over and over.
examples: Astronauts on the space station have grown and eaten lettuce they grew there.
The water in your glass may once have been inside a dinosaur or a tree in an ancient forest.
explanations.art: An astronaut floating beside small pillows with lettuce growing from them, wicks drawing water in. In the corner, a star exploding and a drop of water.
explanations.context: This card goes far out: how plants drink in space, and where the water in a plant first came from.

agreed.text: Water travels into a plant through its roots. It goes up the stem in tiny tubes called xylem, and out to the leaves and flowers.
agreed.evidence: Stand a white flower or a celery stalk in coloured water. The colour reaches the petals and leaves, and a cut stem shows coloured dots where the tubes are. Scientists also see the tubes under microscopes.

agreed.text: Most of the water a plant takes up leaves through tiny holes in its leaves, as vapour.
agreed.evidence: A bag tied over a leafy branch fills with mist and drops. Stephen Hales weighed potted plants in 1727 and found they lost a lot of water each day. Plant scientists estimate that more than 90 out of every 100 drops a plant takes up go back into the air.

chart.title: Of every 100 drops a plant takes up, where do they go? (a rough estimate, it varies)

data.label: Out of the leaves into the air: about 97
Kept or used to make food: about 3

agreed.text: Water is pulled up from the top, as it evaporates from the leaves. Water molecules hold together in unbroken threads as they rise.
agreed.evidence: Dixon and Joly proposed this in 1894. Since then, scientists have measured the stretching pull inside the water tubes of many plants. Leafy stems pull water up faster than bare ones.

agreed.text: A plant wilts when it loses water faster than it can take it in.
agreed.evidence: A wilted plant given water stands up again within hours. Plants droop most on hot, dry afternoons.

agreed.text: Sun, warmth, wind and dry air make plants lose water faster.
agreed.evidence: In tests like the sun and shade bag test, the branch in the sun gives off more water. Farmers and gardeners have known this for thousands of years.

challenging.claim: Plants drink mainly through their leaves, so we should pour water over the leaves.
challenging.who: A common idea, especially when people water plants from above
challenging.for: Leaves do get wet in the rain, and a very little water can soak in through leaves.
challenging.against: Almost all the water a plant uses comes in through its roots. Water poured on the leaves mostly runs off or evaporates. Wet leaves in hot sun or at night can even help some plant diseases. Water the soil, near the roots.
challenging.context: This card is about a common habit when watering plants, and whether it really helps the plant drink.

challenging.claim: Living cells in the stem pump water up, like tiny hearts.
challenging.who: Jagadish Chandra Bose, the great Indian scientist, in 1923
challenging.for: Bose's very sensitive instruments recorded tiny rhythmic electrical pulses in the living cells of stems. He believed these pulses were the pump.
challenging.against: In 1891, Eduard Strasburger killed the living cells in long stems, and liquid still climbed up them. The main water tubes are dead cells anyway. Today almost all plant scientists accept the pulling idea of Dixon and Joly instead. Bose was wrong about this, but right about many other things, like plants sensing touch and injury.
challenging.context: This card is about a famous idea from Jagadish Chandra Bose, an Indian scientist, about how water climbs up plants.

challenging.claim: The roots push water all the way to the top of a tree.
challenging.who: An early idea, from the work of Stephen Hales and others
challenging.for: Roots really do push. A cut vine drips sap, and beads of water appear on grass tips in the morning.
challenging.against: Root pressure is small. It can push water a few metres at most, and many trees have none at all in summer. It cannot lift water 100 metres up a redwood. The pull from the leaves does most of the work.
challenging.context: This card is about the idea that roots push water up a plant, and why it cannot explain tall trees.

challenging.claim: Water climbs a stem the way tea climbs a tissue, by capillary action alone.
challenging.who: Many children, and some older books
challenging.for: Water does creep up thin gaps by itself, and plant tubes are very thin.
challenging.against: Capillary action alone can only lift water a short way in tubes as wide as a plant's, much less than the height of a tall tree. It helps water cling to the tube walls, but the big lift comes from the pull of evaporation at the leaves.
challenging.context: Tea climbs up a tissue dipped in it. This card asks whether that is how water climbs a tree.

challenging.claim: Plants waste water by letting most of it escape from their leaves.
challenging.who: A common way of seeing it, especially in dry places
challenging.for: Most of the water a plant takes up does go straight back into the air.
challenging.against: The plant must open its leaf holes to let in air for making food, and water escapes whenever they are open. The escaping water also cools the leaves, pulls minerals up from the soil, and returns water to the sky as rain. Scientists see it as a price the plant pays, not a waste.
challenging.context: Most of the water a plant drinks escapes into the air. This card asks whether that is a waste.

challenging.claim: Thirsty plants click, and animals or other plants can hear it and learn something.
challenging.who: Lilach Hadany's team in Tel Aviv, as an idea to test, after their 2023 study
challenging.for: The clicks are real and were recorded from about 10 centimetres away. Some moths and mice hear sounds this high.
challenging.against: Nobody has yet shown any animal or plant listening to these clicks or acting on them. They may just be a side effect of air bubbles forming.
challenging.context: In 2023, scientists recorded thirsty plants making tiny clicks. This card asks whether anything is listening.

big_questions.q: A tree has no heart and no pump. How can it lift water higher than a house, every single day?
big_questions.hint: Think about the line of children holding hands up the stairs. Who is doing the pulling?

big_questions.q: Why does a thread of water not snap when it is pulled up a tall tree?
big_questions.hint: Try floating a paperclip on water, or filling a tumbler until the water bulges over the top.

big_questions.q: The water in your glass may once have been inside a dinosaur, a cloud and a mango tree. Who does water really belong to?
big_questions.hint: Where was this water last week? Where will it be next year?

big_questions.q: A plant lets almost all of its water go. Is letting go always a loss?
big_questions.hint: What does the escaping water do for the leaf, and for the rain far away?

big_questions.q: Jagadish Chandra Bose was one of India's greatest scientists, and he was wrong about how water climbs. Can a great scientist be wrong? Does that make them less great?
big_questions.hint: What did other scientists do with his idea? How do we find out who is right?

big_questions.q: You cannot see water climbing inside a stem. So how can you be sure it does?
big_questions.hint: What did the coloured water show you? What is evidence?

big_questions.q: Thirsty plants make clicks too high for us to hear. What else might be happening around us that our senses miss?
big_questions.hint: Think of sounds dogs hear, colours bees see, and smells ants follow.

big_questions.q: If all the trees in a forest are cut, the rain can change far away. Who should decide whether a forest is cut?
big_questions.hint: Think of the farmers who live where the rain falls, and the people who want the wood.

big_questions.q: Why can moss only grow a few millimetres tall, while a tree can grow taller than a 30-storey building?
big_questions.hint: What does a tree have inside it that moss does not?

big_questions.q: Your heart pushes your blood. A tree is pulled by the Sun. Could anything living be powered by the Sun, like a tree?
big_questions.hint: Where does the energy in your food first come from?

big_questions.q: A banyan tree can live for hundreds of years, drinking every day. How many buckets of water do you think it has lifted in its life?
big_questions.hint: Think of hundreds of litres a day, for every day of hundreds of years.

story.title: Blue Before Morning
story.note: Mullick Ghat flower market under Howrah Bridge in Kolkata is real, and flower sellers really do colour white flowers by standing their stems in coloured water. Cutting stems again under water is a real florists' trick to stop air getting into the tubes. Rumki, her mother, Ismail Chacha and the wedding order are made up.
text: Under the great iron bridge in Kolkata, where the river slides past brown and slow, there is a flower market that never sleeps. Marigolds lie in orange hills. Roses come in wet sacks. And at the far end, where the steps go down to the water, Rumki's mother had a stall no wider than a bed.
Rumki was ten. She could tie a marigold garland faster than she could say her eight times table. But on the evening of this story, there was no time for garlands.

A man in a shiny shirt had come to the stall. 'My daughter is getting married tomorrow,' he said. 'She wants blue flowers. Blue like the sky over her grandmother's village. Three hundred stems of rajnigandha, blue, by six in the morning.' He put down more money than Rumki had ever seen her mother hold. 'Can you do it?'
Rajnigandha is white. Its flowers are small and waxy and smell of night. Nobody grows a blue one.
'I can do it,' said Rumki's mother.
Rumki stared at her. Her mother only winked.

That evening they bought three hundred stems from a farmer whose cart had stood in the sun all afternoon. The stems were a little tired. Then Rumki ran to Bhola-da's sweet shop and came back with four small bottles of blue food colour, the kind he used for his sugar birds. They filled two plastic buckets with water, poured in the colour until it was dark as ink, and stood the stems inside. Then they carried the buckets into the little back room behind the stall, where it was warm and quiet, and shut the door so that nobody would knock them over.
'Now the flowers will drink,' said her mother. 'By morning, they will drink the blue right up into their petals.'
Rumki fell asleep on a pile of empty sacks.
When she woke, it was midnight. The market was humming. Her mother was holding a lantern over the buckets, and her face was the wrong shape.
The flowers were white. Not a single petal had a speck of blue.
'They are not drinking,' her mother whispered. 'I have done this a hundred times. Why aren't they drinking?'

Rumki looked at the stems standing in the dark blue water. They looked as if they were waiting for something. She thought of the farmer's cart, and the stems lying in a heap in the hot afternoon sun, their cut ends open to the air.
And she thought of Ismail Chacha.

Ismail Chacha had the stall next to theirs. He made the long white garlands for weddings, and he was very old and very slow, and he did one thing that had always made Rumki laugh. Before he put any flower into water, he held its stem under the water in his big tin tub. Then he cut the end off, there, under the water, with his little curved knife. Never in the air. Always under the water.
'Why do you do that, Chacha?' she had asked him once.

'So the stem doesn't swallow air,' he had said. 'A stem is a bundle of tiny pipes, beti, finer than your hair. Inside each pipe is one long thread of water, all the way up to the flower. If air gets in at the bottom, the thread breaks. Then the flower can pull and pull, and nothing comes.'
Rumki had thought he was telling her a story. Now she looked at the white flowers, and her heart started to race.
'Ma,' she said. 'Bring the knife.'

So that is what they did, in the middle of the night. Rumki held each stem down under the blue water, and her mother cut a finger's width off the bottom with the kitchen knife. Snip, under the water. Three hundred times. Their arms went blue to the elbow.

But when they had finished, the room was still hot and still, and the air was thick and wet, like the inside of a cooking pot with the lid on. Rumki thought of the washing on the roof. Her mother always said clothes dried fastest in the wind off the river, and slowest on a still, wet day. If the flowers had to let water go, to pull more water up behind it, then they needed somewhere to let it go to.
'The roof,' she said. 'Ma, they need the wind.'

They carried the heavy buckets up the narrow stairs, one by one, slopping blue onto the steps. On the roof, the river wind came off the water, cool and steady, and it moved through the white flowers like a hand through hair. Rumki sat beside the buckets with her knees under her chin. She watched the lights of the bridge. She did not sleep.

At about four o'clock, when the sky was the colour of a pigeon's wing, she saw it. At the very edge of one petal, a thin blue line, as fine as a thread. Then another. Then, as she looked closer, she saw that each petal had tiny blue roads running through it, branching and branching, like the map of a city. The blue was climbing the pipes. It was following the water to the place where the water left, into the wind.
By six o'clock, three hundred rajnigandha stood in the buckets, white at the centre, blue at every edge and every vein, as if someone had drawn them with a pen made of sky.

The man in the shiny shirt came. He looked at the flowers for a long time and said nothing. Then he paid, and he gave Rumki an extra ten rupees, and he carried the buckets to his car very carefully, the way people carry babies.
When he had gone, Ismail Chacha shuffled over to look at the blue drips on the stairs. 'Under the water?' he asked.
'Under the water,' said Rumki. 'And then the wind.'
The old man nodded, as if this was the most ordinary thing in the world. Then he went back to his tub, held a stem under the water, and cut.
story.epiphany: For the parent: the flowers do not drink the colour because they are standing in it. They drink because water leaves the petals into the air and pulls more water up the stem behind it. Two things stop that pull in the story. Air got into the cut ends while the stems lay in the sun, and broke the threads of water in the tubes. And the hot, still, damp back room gave the water nowhere to evaporate. Cutting the stems under water mends the threads. The river wind lets the water leave. Then the blue climbs, and shows the hidden roads inside every petal. The story also notices the quiet expert at the next stall, whose habit everyone laughed at.
ask: The flowers stood in blue water for hours and stayed white. Why do you think they were not drinking?
Why did Ismail Chacha always cut stems under the water, never in the air?
Why did Rumki carry the buckets up to the windy roof?
What did the thin blue lines in the petals show Rumki?
Ismail Chacha's habit looked silly to Rumki at first. Do you know someone whose careful habits turned out to be wise?

printables.title: 4 water drop counters, one for each player

rules: Each player is a drop of water. Put your drop on square 1, in the soil.
On your turn, roll a dice and move that many squares.
Whenever you land on a square with a star, take a card and do what it says.
Read the name of each part out loud as you pass into it: soil, root hairs, root, stem, veins, leaf hole, air, rain.
The first drop to fall back into the soil as rain, on square 30, wins.
After the game, everyone tells the whole journey of their drop in their own words.

flow.do: 1. Lay the board on the floor. 2. Shuffle the cards and put them face down. 3. Give each player a drop counter on square 1.
flow.say: Each of us is a drop of water in the soil, under a plant. Let's race through the plant and back up into the sky.
flow.kid: You are a drop of water in the soil. Put your drop on square 1. Race through the plant to the sky and back!
flow.context: This is the first step of Drop's Journey. It is a board game. Each player is a drop of water travelling through a plant, from soil to leaf to sky.

flow.do: Before rolling, trace the whole path on the board together with one finger, saying each part's name.
flow.say: First, let's trace the road. Soil. Root hairs. Root. Stem. Veins. Leaf hole. Air. Rain. Which part comes straight after the root?
flow.kid: Trace the road with your finger. Say each part. Soil, root hairs, root, stem, veins, leaf hole, air, rain.

check.q: In Drop's Journey, which part does the drop reach straight after the root?
options: The leaf
The stem
The flower
check.why: Water goes from the roots into the stem, and climbs the stem's tubes before it reaches any leaf or flower. Picking the leaf usually means skipping the stem, as if water jumped straight from root to leaf.

flow.do: 1. Take turns rolling and moving. 2. When someone lands on a star, they read a card out loud. 3. Before they move, ask them to say why the card makes sense.
flow.say: You got 'Hot sunny afternoon, move ahead 3'. Why would a hot sun make a drop move faster?
flow.kid: Roll and move. Landed on a star? Take a card and read it. Say why it makes sense. Then move.

ask.q: Why does the air bubble card send you back?
good: The bubble breaks the thread of water, so it can't be pulled up.
A tube with air in it can't carry water.

ask.q: Why does night make you miss a turn?
good: The leaf holes close at night.
Less water leaves the leaves when it is dark and cool.

flow.parent: Good reasons: sun, warmth, wind and dry air make leaves lose water faster, and that pulls water up faster. Night, mist and closed leaf holes slow it down. Torn root hairs mean the plant cannot drink.

flow.do: When the game ends, each player tells the full journey of their drop, in order, without looking at the board.
flow.say: Tell me your drop's whole journey, from the soil to the sky and back. What happened on the way?
flow.kid: Tell the story of your drop. Where did it start? Where did it go? How did it get back to the soil?
flow.think: The drop went back into the soil as rain. Could it go through the same plant again? Could it go through you?

games.context: This is a board game about the journey of a drop of water. It goes into a plant's roots and up the stem. Then it goes out through a leaf into the sky, and back down as rain.

rules: Each leaf player puts their two hands together, palms touching. The hands are the two guard cells around a leaf hole.
Open the hole by bending your hands apart into a round shape. Close it by pressing them together.
The caller reads a card. Each leaf decides fast: open or close? Show it with your hands.
The caller asks one leaf to say why. A good reason wins a point.
Open holes let air in for making food, but let water out. Closed holes save water, but let no air in. Think about both.
After 12 cards, the leaf with the most points wins.

flow.do: Show your child how to make a leaf hole with two hands. Bend the hands apart to open, press them together to close.
flow.say: Every leaf has thousands of tiny holes. Each one has two curved cells around it, like your two hands. They open the hole or close it.
flow.kid: Put your hands together. They are two guard cells. Bend them apart to open the hole. Press them together to close it.
flow.context: This is the first step of Open or Close?. In this game, your two hands are the guard cells around a tiny leaf hole. They open and close to let air in and water out.

flow.do: Play the first card together as practice: 'Hot afternoon, soil is very dry'.
flow.say: Hot afternoon, and the soil is very dry. Open or close? Think about the water.
flow.kid: Practice card: hot afternoon, very dry soil. Open or close? Show your hands.

check.q: Hot afternoon, and the soil is very dry. What do the leaf holes usually do?
options: Open wide to cool down
Close, to save water
Nothing changes
check.why: When the soil is dry, the roots cannot replace the water fast enough. If the holes stayed open, the plant would wilt or even dry out. So most plants close their holes, even though this stops air coming in. Picking 'open wide to cool down' is a good thought, because evaporation does cool a leaf. But a plant with no water to spare must save it first.

flow.do: 1. Play the rest of the cards. 2. After each one, ask a leaf to say why. 3. Give a point for any reason that mentions water or air.
flow.say: Bright morning sun, soil is wet. Open or close? Why?
flow.kid: Listen to each card. Open or close? Show your hands fast. Then say why.
flow.parent: Usual answers: open in bright light with wet soil. The leaf needs air to make food, and has water to spare. Close at night, because there is no light to make food. Close in a heatwave or drought, to save water. A cactus closes in the day and opens at night, when it is cooler and less water escapes. A plant in a bag full of damp air can open. Little water leaves, because the air is already wet.

flow.do: Talk about the hardest card.
flow.say: Which card was hardest to decide? Why is it hard for a plant to choose?
flow.kid: Which card was hardest? Why is it hard for a plant to choose?
flow.think: A plant must let some water go to get the air it needs. Do people ever have to give up something to get something else?

items.p: Put the path of water through a plant in order, from start to end: stem, air, root hairs, leaf, root.
items.why: Root hairs soak up the water, and it moves into the root. It climbs the stem and spreads through the leaf. Then it leaves into the air as vapour.

items.p: Which part of a plant soaks up water from the soil?
items.why: Roots, and especially their tiny root hairs, soak up water from the soil. Picking 'leaves' usually comes from seeing people water plants from above. Leaves let water out. They do not take much in.
items.art: A plant pulled up gently, its fuzzy roots dripping.

items.p: The tiny water tubes inside a stem are called ____.
items.why: Xylem tubes carry water from the roots up to the leaves and flowers.

items.p: A white flower stood in blue water overnight. In the morning its petals had blue edges. What does this show?
opts: Water travelled up the stem into the petals
The blue soaked through the air
items.why: The colour can only reach the petals by travelling with the water, up the stem. Picking 'soaked through the air' usually means not noticing that the petals never touched the blue water.
items.context: In the Blue Climb experiment, you stand a white flower or a celery stalk in coloured water. Then you watch where the colour goes.

items.p: Most of the water a plant takes in leaves again through tiny holes in its leaves.
items.why: True. More than 90 out of every 100 drops go back into the air as vapour. This is called transpiration.

items.p: Water leaving a plant's leaves as invisible vapour is called ____.
items.why: Transpiration is water leaving the leaves. It pulls more water up the stem.

items.p: In the Sweating Branch test, which bag collected more water?
items.why: Sun warms the leaves and they let out more water vapour, which turns back into drops on the bag. Picking 'the shade' usually means thinking cool places are wetter. But these drops came out of the plant.
items.context: In the Sweating Branch test, you tie clear bags over two leafy branches. One is in the sun and one is in the shade. The bags catch the water the leaves let out.

items.p: Match each word to what it means.
pairs: soaks up water from the soil
a tiny hole in a leaf
a line on a leaf that holds water tubes
items.why: Root hairs soak water in, xylem carries it up, veins spread it through the leaf, and stomata let it out.

items.p: A balsam plant is drooping on a hot afternoon. What is most likely happening?
opts: It is losing water from its leaves faster than its roots can drink
items.why: Wilting means the plant is losing water faster than it can take it in, so its cells go soft. Picking 'sleeping' is a fun idea. Some plants do fold their leaves at night, but that is different from wilting in the heat.

items.p: Sort these. Do they make a plant lose water FASTER or SLOWER?
items.why: Sun, warmth, wind, dry air and many leaves all speed up water loss. Cool, still, damp air and closed holes slow it down. It is like drying clothes.

items.p: The roots push water all the way to the top of a tall tree.
items.why: False. Roots push only a little. Most of the lift comes from the leaves letting water evaporate, which pulls the water up.

items.p: Why do flower sellers cut stems again under water?
opts: To make the stems shorter for the vase
To stop air bubbles getting into the water tubes and blocking them
items.why: Air in a tube breaks its thread of water, so that tube stops carrying water. Cutting under water keeps air out. Picking 'shorter for the vase' is partly true, but the 'under water' part is about bubbles.

items.p: In the Leafy or Bare test, the stem with ____ drank much more water.
items.why: The leaves let water out into the air, and that pulls more water up the stem. The bare stem has nothing to let the water out.
items.context: In the Leafy or Bare test, two stems stand in two bottles of water with oil on top. One stem has leaves and one has none. You measure how far each water level drops.

items.p: Tell the story of one drop of water, from the soil to the sky. Use the words root, stem and leaf.
items.a: My drop was in the wet soil. A root hair soaked it up into the root. It climbed up the stem through a tiny tube. It went along a vein in a leaf. Then it went out of a tiny hole and floated into the air as vapour.
items.why: A full answer has the parts in the right order: root, stem, leaf, air.

items.p: Your friend says, 'I water my plant by spraying the leaves.' What would you tell them, and why?
items.a: I would tell them to water the soil, near the roots. Plants drink through their roots, not their leaves. Most of the water on the leaves just runs off or dries away.
items.why: Any answer that says to water the soil, because roots do the drinking, is right.

items.p: Draw a plant in a pot. Draw blue arrows to show the path of water from the soil to the air. Label root, stem, leaf and air.
items.a: Arrows start in the soil, go into the roots, up the stem, along the leaves, and out of the leaves into the air.
items.why: The arrows should go one way, upwards, and end in the air.
items.art: An outline of a potted plant for the child to draw arrows on.

items.p: When you cut a celery stalk across after the Blue Climb, you see a row of coloured dots. What are the dots?
items.why: Each dot is a bundle of xylem tubes, which the coloured water climbed through. Picking 'drops of paint' means thinking the colour just sits in the stem. It is inside tubes, which is why it shows as dots.
items.context: In the Blue Climb experiment, you stand a white flower or a celery stalk in coloured water. Then you watch where the colour goes.

items.p: In the Leafy or Bare test, why did we pour a thin layer of oil on the water?
opts: So water could not evaporate from the bottle itself
items.why: The oil is a lid. Then any water that disappears must have gone up the stem. Picking 'to feed the stems' means thinking plants eat what is in their water.
items.context: In the Leafy or Bare test, two stems stand in two bottles of water with oil on top. One stem has leaves and one has none. You measure how far each water level drops.

items.p: In the Leafy or Bare test, the leafy stem's water dropped 18 mm and the bare stem's dropped 3 mm. How many times more did the leafy stem drink?
items.why: 18 divided by 3 is 6. So the leafy stem drank 6 times as much. Picking 15 means taking away instead of dividing. 18 take away 3 is 15 mm more, which is also true, but it does not say how many times.
items.context: In the Leafy or Bare test, two stems stand in two bottles of water with oil on top. One stem has leaves and one has none. You measure how far each water level drops.

chart.title: Made-up example: water level drop in 2 days

items.p: Water molecules hold on to each other. What is this called?
items.why: Cohesion means water sticking to itself. It lets a thread of water be pulled up a tube without snapping. Picking 'evaporation' mixes up the pull at the top with what holds the thread together.

items.p: Where does the energy to lift water up a tree mostly come from?
opts: The Sun, which makes water evaporate from the leaves
The roots, which pump very hard
items.why: Sunlight warms the leaves and makes water evaporate, and that pulls the water up. Trees have no heart. Picking 'the wind' is close, because wind helps water leave faster, but the Sun gives most of the energy.

items.p: A tree can lift water much higher than any suction pump can.
items.why: True. Suction can lift water only about 10 metres. The tallest tree is about 116 metres. The tree pulls from the top using cohesion, not air pushing.

items.p: A white flower's stem was split in two. One half stood in blue water and one in red. What happened?
opts: The flower went purple all over
One side of the flower went blue and the other side red
items.why: Each tube carries water to its own part of the flower. The tubes do not mix. Picking 'purple' is a sensible guess, because the stem looks like one thing. The flower shows it is many separate tubes.
items.context: In the Two-Colour Flower activity, a grown-up splits the bottom of a white flower's stem into two halves. Each half stands in a different colour.

items.p: Match each person to their idea about how water climbs.
pairs: weighed plants and showed leaves lose lots of water
showed water climbs even when stem cells are killed
water is pulled up from the top and holds together
living cells pump water up, like tiny hearts
items.why: These four scientists each added a piece to the puzzle. Today, the pulling idea of Dixon and Joly is accepted.

items.p: On a hot, dry afternoon, many plants close their leaf holes. Why?
items.why: Closing the holes stops water escaping when the plant is short of it. It also stops air coming in, so the plant makes less food then. Picking 'to make more food' is the opposite: closed holes mean less food.

items.p: Is the water drop from INSIDE the plant or from the AIR?
items: one round drop at the tip of a grass blade at dawn
tiny drops all over a leaf on a cold morning
drops inside a bag tied over a branch
drops on the outside of a cold steel tumbler
items.why: Drops at grass tips are pushed out by the roots, and drops in the bag came out of the leaves. Dew and drops on a cold tumbler form from water vapour in the air.

items.p: A plant goes floppy when its cells lose water. This is called ____.
items.why: Wilting happens when water leaves faster than it comes in, and the cells go soft.

items.p: In the Water Chain play, one person in the middle let go of hands. Why did the people below them stop moving up?
opts: Nothing was pulling them any more, like a broken thread of water
items.why: The pull from the top only travels along joined hands. An air bubble breaks a real water thread in the same way. Picking 'the roots stopped pushing' means thinking roots do the main work.
items.context: In the Water Chain play, people hold hands up a staircase. They act out water being pulled up a tube in a plant.

items.p: Mosses are small partly because they have no proper water tubes.
items.why: True. Without strong tubes to carry water up, mosses stay low, close to damp ground.

items.p: Why does a plant need its leaf holes open, even though water escapes through them?
items.a: The plant needs air to come in through the holes, so the leaves can make food. When the holes open, water vapour escapes too. The escaping water also pulls more water up and cools the leaf.
items.why: A good answer says the holes let air in for making food, and water escapes at the same time.

items.p: Imagine a plant with no leaves at all. Would water still climb up its stem? Explain using the Leafy or Bare test.
items.a: Only a little. In the Leafy or Bare test, the bare stem drank only 3 mm, but the leafy stem drank 18 mm. Without leaves, there is almost nowhere for the water to leave, so almost nothing pulls it up.
items.why: A good answer uses the evidence from the test and says the leaves do the pulling.
items.context: In the Leafy or Bare test, two stems stand in two bottles of water with oil on top. One stem has leaves and one has none. You measure how far each water level drops.

items.p: In 1891, Eduard Strasburger killed all the living cells in long stems, and coloured water still climbed up them. Which idea did this show to be wrong?
opts: Water is pulled up by evaporation from the leaves
Living cells must pump water up the stem
items.why: If living pumps were needed, a dead stem could not lift water. But it did. So living pumps are not needed. Picking 'pulled by evaporation' misses that a dead stem can still let water evaporate from its top.

items.p: Jagadish Chandra Bose thought living cells pump water up stems. Most scientists now think he was wrong about this. What is the best thing to say about Bose?
opts: He was a great scientist who was wrong about one idea, as all scientists sometimes are
He was right and everyone else is wrong
items.why: Being wrong about one idea is a normal part of science. Bose made great discoveries about how plants sense and respond, and about radio waves. Picking 'bad scientist' means thinking good scientists are never wrong. Science moves forward by testing ideas, including great people's ideas.

items.p: A suction pump can lift water about 10 metres. The tallest tree, Hyperion, is about 116 metres. About how many times taller is the tree than the suction limit?
items.why: 116 divided by 10 is about 11.6, so about 11 times. Picking 100 times usually comes from adding the zero of 10 to the answer by mistake.

items.p: In 2023, scientists recorded thirsty tomato plants making tiny clicks. What do most scientists think causes the clicks?
opts: The plant is crying for help on purpose
Water threads snapping and air bubbles forming in the tubes
items.why: When a plant is very thirsty, its water threads are stretched very hard. Some snap, and a tiny air bubble forms with a click. Picking 'crying for help on purpose' is a big question nobody has answered. There is no evidence the plant means anything by it.

items.p: Scientists all agree on exactly how much of the rain over land comes from water that plants send up.
items.why: False. One study in 2013 said plants send up about 80 to 90 out of every 100 drops rising from land. Later studies said about 60. They agree it is a big share, but not on the exact amount.

items.p: A redwood's leaves at the very top are much smaller than its lower leaves. What might that tell scientists?
opts: Water barely reaches the top, so the top leaves stay small and thirsty
items.why: George Koch's team found the top leaves of the tallest redwoods were small and thirsty. It was as if water could barely be pulled that high. This helped them estimate how tall a tree can grow. Picking 'less light' is wrong, because the top gets the most light of all.

items.p: Put these in order, from the one that lifts water LEAST high to the one that lifts it MOST high: a tall tree, a suction pump, a paper towel.
items.why: A paper towel lifts water a few centimetres by capillary action. A suction pump lifts it up to about 10 metres. A tall tree lifts it over 100 metres, by pulling from the top.

items.p: Astronauts on the space station grow plants in small pillows with wicks. Why?
opts: In space, water does not drip down into the soil, so wicks bring it to the roots
Plants in space do not need water
The pillows keep the plants warm
To stop the plants floating off
items.why: On Earth, gravity pulls water down around the roots. In space, water floats in clumps. A wick moves water by capillary action, which works without gravity. Picking 'to stop floating off' is partly true for the plants, but the wicks are for the water.

items.p: Is this a PUSH from the roots or a PULL from the leaves?
items: sap dripping from a cut vine stump
water climbing fastest on a hot sunny afternoon
a drop at a grass tip at dawn
the leafy stem drinking more than the bare stem
items.why: Dripping stumps and dawn drops at grass tips show the small push from the roots. Fast drinking in the sun and the leafy stem show the much bigger pull from the leaves.

items.p: A forest is cut down. Months later, the farms downwind get less rain. Which explanation fits best?
opts: The trees were sending lots of water up into the air, which used to fall as rain further along
The farmers used up all the rain
Cutting trees makes the Sun hotter
There is no link at all
items.why: Trees send huge amounts of water into the air through their leaves. Some of it forms clouds and rain further along. Without the trees, less water goes up. Picking 'no link at all' would be fair if we had no evidence. But scientists have measured this in places like the Amazon.

items.p: The tiny electric pulls that hold water molecules together are called hydrogen ____.
items.why: Hydrogen bonds join the hydrogen end of one water molecule to the oxygen end of the next.

items.p: Why is the air under a big neem tree cooler than in a sunny car park, even apart from the shade?
opts: Water evaporating from the leaves takes heat away, like sweat drying on skin
Leaves blow cold air like a fan
items.why: Turning water into vapour takes heat energy. The leaves give it up, so they and the air around them cool down. Picking 'blow like a fan' is close, because moving leaves do stir the air, but the main cooling is evaporation.

items.p: In Be Stephen Hales, a plant weighed 480 grams on Tuesday and 466 grams on Wednesday, a cloudy day. On Monday to Tuesday, a sunny day, it lost 32 grams. Which day did it lose more, and why?
opts: The sunny day, because water evaporates faster in sun
The cloudy day, because clouds pull water
The cloudy day, because it was 14 grams
items.why: 480 take away 466 is 14 grams on the cloudy day, less than 32 grams on the sunny day. Sun makes leaves lose water faster. Picking 'the cloudy day, because it was 14 grams' means finding the right number but comparing it the wrong way.
items.context: In the Be Stephen Hales project, you cover a pot's soil so water can only leave through the leaves. Then you weigh the plant every day.

items.p: The water in your glass may once have been inside a dinosaur, a cloud and a tree. Explain how the same water could have been in all three.
items.a: Water goes round and round. A tree pulls water up and lets it out into the air. It becomes a cloud and falls as rain. A dinosaur drinks it and breathes it out. The same water keeps travelling for millions of years.
items.why: A good answer describes water moving between living things, the air and rain, again and again.

items.p: Bose was a great scientist, and he was wrong about how water climbs. What does this tell you about how science works?
items.a: Even great scientists can be wrong. Other scientists test their ideas. When the evidence shows an idea is wrong, science changes, even if the person was famous. Being wrong is part of finding out.
items.why: Any answer that says ideas are tested with evidence, and that anyone can be wrong, is right.

items.p: Design a fair test to find out whether wind makes a plant lose water faster. Say what you will change, what you will keep the same, and what you will measure.
items.a: I will use two similar leafy stems in two identical bottles with oil on top. One will be in front of a fan, the other in the same room with no fan. I will keep the light, the warmth and the stems the same. I will measure how far the water drops in each bottle after a day.
items.why: A good answer changes only the wind, keeps everything else the same, and measures the water used.

experiments.title: The Blue Climb: coloured water up a stem
experiments.question: How does water travel from the bottom of a stem to the leaves and flowers? Where does it go, and how fast?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Will the colour go up the stem? Will it reach the leaves and petals? How long will it take? Draw your guess.
experiments.fair_test: To compare, stand one stem in plain water and one in coloured water. Use the same kind of stem, cut the same way, in the same place. Only the colour of the water is different. Check both at the same times.
results_table: How far up the stem the colour has climbed (cm)
What the leaves or petals look like

materials.item: 2 white flowers with long stems, such as rajnigandha, white chrysanthemum or white rose, or 2 celery stalks with leaves, or 2 balsam plants pulled up gently with roots
2 clear glasses or jars
dark blue or red food colour
a kitchen knife, for a grown-up only
a ruler, a clock and a pencil
a magnifying glass, if you have one

experiments.safety: A grown-up does all the cutting. Food colour stains clothes and hands, so put newspaper down.

schedule.what: Guess, set up the two glasses, and check at 1 hour and before bed.
Look in the morning. A grown-up cuts the stem across. Look at the coloured dots and pull out a coloured string. Draw and finish.

experiments.record: Fill in the table at each check. Draw the stem, the leaves or petals, and the cut end of the stem.

flow.do: 1. Fill both glasses halfway with water. 2. Stir about 20 drops of food colour into one glass, until it is dark. 3. Ask your child to draw a guess of what will happen.
flow.say: This glass has coloured water and this one has plain water. If we stand a white flower in the coloured water, what do you think will happen? Draw your guess.
flow.kid: Put water in two glasses. Add lots of colour to one. What will happen to a white flower in it? Draw your guess.

ask.q: Where do you think the colour will go?
good: Up the stem.
Into the petals.
It will stay in the glass.

flow.parent: Any guess is fine. A child who says 'it will stay in the glass' has a clear idea that we can test. Do not correct it yet.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Blue Climb. You stand white flowers or celery in coloured water and watch where the water goes.

flow.do: 1. Hold the bottom of each stem under water in a bowl. Cut about 2 cm off it at a slant, under the water. 2. Stand one stem in each glass straight away. 3. Write down the time.
flow.say: I'm cutting the stems under water, so no air gets into the tubes. Air bubbles would block them. Now let's write down the time.
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up to cut the stems under water. Stand one in each glass. Write down the time.
flow.parent: Cutting under water is what flower sellers do. A stem cut in the air can take in a little air, which blocks some tubes. If your stems have been lying out for hours, a fresh cut is even more important.

flow.do: 1. After 1 hour, look closely at the stem and the petals or leaves. 2. If the stem is see-through, like balsam, measure how high the colour has climbed with the ruler. 3. Write it in the table. 4. Look again before bed.
flow.say: Let's look. Can you see colour anywhere yet? Where is it? Let's measure how high it has gone.
flow.kid: After one hour, look closely. Where is the colour? Measure how high it has climbed. Write it down.

good: No, it is still white.
No. So the colour came from the water.

flow.parent: Balsam stems are see-through, so you can watch the colour rise. In celery and flowers, colour often shows first at the leaf tips and petal edges, after a few hours. Slow results are normal. A warm, airy room speeds it up.

flow.do: In the morning, look at the petals or leaves with the magnifying glass. Draw what you see.
flow.say: Look at the petals now. Where is the colour darkest? What do the lines look like?
flow.kid: Good morning! Look at the petals or leaves. Where is the colour darkest? Draw the lines you see.

check.q: In the Blue Climb, the white petals now have coloured lines and edges. What does that show?
options: The flower changed colour by itself overnight
Water climbed up the stem and spread through tiny tubes into the petals
The colour soaked in through the outside of the petals
check.why: The only way the colour could reach the petals is with the water, up through the stem. The plain-water flower stayed white, so the flower did not change by itself. The petals never touched the coloured water, so it did not soak in from outside. Picking 'by itself' usually means the plain-water flower was not compared. That is why we set up two glasses.

flow.wait: Leave the stems overnight, at least 12 hours.

flow.do: 1. Cut across the stem about halfway up. 2. Look at the cut end with the magnifying glass. 3. For celery, snap a piece and pull out one of the coloured strings.
flow.say: Look at the cut end. Can you see coloured dots? Each dot is a bundle of tiny tubes. The water climbed up through them. Now let's pull one out.
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up to cut the stem across. Look at the end. See the coloured dots? Each one is a bundle of water tubes!

ask.q: Why are there dots, and not colour everywhere?
good: The water only went up the tubes.
The tubes are in bundles, not everywhere.

flow.parent: In celery the dots sit in a curved row near the outside. In a flower stem they are often in a ring. These are the xylem bundles. A coloured string pulled from celery is a bundle of xylem tubes.

flow.do: Look at the table together. Ask how fast the colour climbed.
flow.say: The colour climbed this far in one hour, and this far by the morning. How many centimetres did it climb each hour?
flow.kid: Look at your table. How far did the colour climb in one hour? How far by morning?
flow.think: A neem tree has no glass of coloured water. Its water tubes are hidden in its wood. How could you find out how fast water climbs in a tree?

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Let's finish like real scientists. Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Finish like a scientist. Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: water climbs up a stem through tiny tubes and goes into the leaves and petals. What I saw: the colour climbed 3 cm in the first hour. The petals got blue edges, and the cut stem had blue dots. The plain flower stayed white. Why: the water carried the colour with it up the tubes, to where it leaves the petals.

experiments.context: This is the coloured-water experiment. You stand a white flower or a celery stalk in coloured water. The colour shows you the hidden path that water takes up a plant.
