experiments.title: Leafy or Bare? Which stem drinks more?
experiments.question: Do the leaves help to pull water up a stem? Does a leafy stem drink more than a bare one?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Will a stem with leaves drink more, less, or the same as a stem with its leaves pulled off?
experiments.fair_test: Use two stems from the same plant, the same length. Put them in two bottles that are exactly the same, with the same amount of water, in the same place. Pour a thin layer of oil on the water in both. Then no water can evaporate from the bottle itself. Only one thing is different: one stem keeps its leaves.

materials.item: 2 leafy stems from the same plant, about the same size, such as tulsi, money plant, hibiscus or coleus
2 identical narrow clear bottles or test tubes
a spoon of cooking oil
a marker pen and a ruler with millimetres

experiments.safety: A grown-up cuts the stems. Wipe up any oil spills, as they make the floor slippery.

schedule.what: Guess. Cut two stems, pull the leaves off one, set up the bottles with oil, and mark the water levels.
Mark and measure the new water levels.
Measure again, draw a bar chart, and finish.

experiments.record: Fill in the table each day. Draw a bar chart with one bar for each stem, as tall as its total drop in millimetres.

flow.do: Ask your child to guess which stem will drink more, and to write the guess down.
flow.say: We'll put two stems in water. One keeps its leaves. One has its leaves taken off. Which one will drink more water? Why?
flow.kid: Two stems in water. One has leaves. One has none. Which will drink more? Write your guess.
flow.context: This is the first step of Leafy or Bare?. You test whether a stem with leaves pulls up more water than a stem with no leaves.

flow.do: 1. Cut two similar stems, each about 20 cm long, under water. 2. Pull all the leaves off one stem. 3. Fill both bottles with the same amount of water. 4. Put one stem in each. 5. Pour a thin layer of oil on the water in each bottle. 6. Mark the water level on each bottle with the marker.
flow.say: The oil is a lid. It stops water drying straight out of the bottle. So any water that goes must go through the stem.
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up to cut two stems. Pull the leaves off one. Put each in a bottle. Add a little oil on top. Mark the water level.

check.q: In the Leafy or Bare test, why do we pour oil on top of the water?
options: To feed the stems
So water can't evaporate from the bottle itself, only through the stem
To make the water heavier
check.why: Water can evaporate from any open surface, even with no plant. A thin oil layer stops that. Then if the water level drops, the water must have gone up the stem. Picking 'to feed the stems' usually means thinking plants eat whatever is put in their water. The oil is only a lid.

flow.do: 1. The next day, mark the new water level on each bottle. 2. Measure the drop from the first mark, in millimetres. 3. Write it in the table.
flow.say: Let's measure. How many millimetres has the water gone down in each bottle?
flow.kid: Mark the new water level. Measure how far it dropped, in millimetres. Write it in the table.
flow.parent: Read the ruler at eye level. Millimetres are the tiny marks between the centimetre numbers. Ten millimetres make one centimetre.

flow.do: 1. On day 3, measure again. 2. Add up the total drop for each stem. 3. Draw a bar chart, one bar for each stem.
flow.say: Let's draw one bar for each stem. Which bar is taller? What does that tell us?
flow.kid: Measure again. Draw one bar for each stem. Which bar is taller?

check.q: In the Leafy or Bare test, the leafy stem's water dropped 18 mm. The bare stem's dropped 3 mm. What does this show?
options: Leaves help pull water up the stem
Bare stems are thirstier
The bottles were different
check.why: Everything was the same except the leaves. The leafy stem used much more water. So the leaves must be what pulls the water up, by letting it escape into the air. Picking 'the bottles were different' is a good worry. That is why we used two bottles that are exactly the same.

flow.do: Talk about why the bare stem still drank a little.
flow.say: The bare stem still drank a tiny bit. Where could that water have gone?
flow.kid: The bare stem drank a tiny bit too. Where did that water go?
flow.parent: A little water evaporates from the stem's skin and the cut top, and a little soaks into the stem. Some stems also have a few leaf holes in the stem's skin.
flow.think: If you pulled most of the leaves off a plant, would it need less water? Why do gardeners sometimes cut back plants when they move them?

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Let's finish like real scientists. Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Finish like a scientist. Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: the leaves pull water up the stem. What I saw: in 2 days the leafy stem's water went down 18 mm. The bare stem's went down only 3 mm. Why: water escapes from the leaves into the air, and that pulls more water up behind it. The bare stem has no leaves to let the water out.

experiments.title: The Sweating Branch: sun or shade?
experiments.question: Does a leafy branch give off more water in the sun or in the shade?
experiments.predict: Guess first. You will tie a clear bag over a branch in the sun, and another over a branch in the shade. Which bag will collect more water?
experiments.fair_test: Use two branches of the same kind of plant, about the same size, with about the same number of leaves. Use two bags that are the same. Tie them on at the same time and leave them for the same time. Only one thing is different: sun or shade.
results_table: What the inside of the bag looks like
Water collected (spoons, or millilitres with a syringe)

materials.item: 2 clear plastic bags of the same size, without holes
2 pieces of thread or rubber bands
2 similar leafy branches still on their plants, one in the sun and one in the shade
a teaspoon, or a medicine syringe without a needle, to measure the water

experiments.safety: Plastic bags are never for heads or faces. Keep them away from very young children. Take the bags off the plants afterwards, so the leaves do not overheat.

schedule.what: Tie the bags on, wait 2 hours, then look, measure and compare.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw both bags, showing the mist and drops inside each one.

flow.do: Find two similar leafy branches, one in bright sun and one in shade. Ask your child to guess which bag will get more water.
flow.say: We're going to catch the water that leaves the leaves. Which bag do you think will get more, the one in the sun or the one in the shade?
flow.kid: Find two leafy branches. One in the sun. One in the shade. Which will give off more water? Guess!
flow.context: This is the first step of the Sweating Branch. You tie clear bags over two leafy branches and catch the water that the leaves let out.

flow.do: 1. Slip a bag over each branch without picking it. 2. Tie the open end loosely but firmly round the branch's stem. 3. Write down the time.
flow.say: Slide the bag over the leaves. Tie it round the stem, not too tight, so we don't hurt the plant.
flow.kid: Slide a bag over each branch. Ask a grown-up to tie it round the stem. Write down the time.

flow.do: 1. After 2 hours, look at both bags without taking them off. 2. Gently tap the drops down into a corner of each bag.
flow.say: Look inside the bags. What do you see? Where did those drops come from?
flow.kid: After two hours, look at the bags. Misty? Drops? Tap the drops into a corner.

ask.q: Where did the water in the bag come from?
good: From the leaves.
It came up the stem and out of the leaves.
Water vapour from the leaves turned back into drops.

flow.do: 1. Take each bag off carefully and pour the water into a spoon or suck it up with the syringe. 2. Write how much each bag collected.
flow.say: Let's measure. How much water came out of each branch in just two hours?
flow.kid: Take the bags off gently. Pour the water into a spoon. Which bag has more?

check.q: In the Sweating Branch test, which bag usually collects more water?
options: The bag on the branch in the sun
The bag on the branch in the shade
Both always get exactly the same
check.why: Sun warms the leaves, makes them open their holes, and makes water evaporate faster. So the sunny branch lets out more water vapour, which turns back into drops on the cool bag. Picking 'the shade' usually means thinking a cool place is wetter, so it would collect more. But the drops come from the plant, not the air.

flow.do: Talk about what this means for a whole tree.
flow.say: This was one small branch, for two hours. A big tree has thousands of branches, all day. How much water do you think a big tree lets out on a hot day?
flow.kid: This was one small branch. A big tree has thousands. How much water does a whole tree let out?
flow.parent: A big tree on a hot day can send up hundreds of litres of water. That is many buckets, lifted by the Sun and let into the air.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Let's finish like real scientists. Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Finish like a scientist. Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: leaves let out more water in the sun. What I saw: the sunny bag had about 2 spoons of water. The shady bag had less than half a spoon. Why: the sun warms the leaves and makes the water evaporate faster, so more water leaves through the leaf holes.

activities.title: The Two-Colour Flower

materials.item: 1 white flower with a long stem, such as rajnigandha, white chrysanthemum or white carnation
2 small glasses, and 2 food colours, such as blue and red
a sharp knife and sticky tape, for a grown-up

activities.safety: Only a grown-up uses the knife. Split the stem slowly, on a chopping board.

schedule.what: Split the stem, stand each half in a different colour, and guess.
Look at the flower in the morning, and draw it.

activities.record: Draw the flower before and after. Colour in where each colour went.

flow.do: 1. Cut the bottom of the stem under water. 2. On a chopping board, split the stem lengthways into two halves. Start at the cut end and stop about halfway up. 3. Wrap a bit of sticky tape round the stem just above the split, so it does not split further.
flow.say: I'm splitting the stem into two legs. One leg will stand in blue water, and the other in red.
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up to split the stem into two legs. Put tape above the split so it stops there.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Two-Colour Flower. You split a white flower's stem into two halves and stand each half in a different colour.

flow.do: 1. Put the two glasses side by side, one blue and one red. 2. Stand one leg of the stem in each glass. 3. Ask your child to guess what the flower will look like in the morning.
flow.say: One leg drinks blue and one drinks red. What will the flower look like tomorrow? Will it go purple? Half and half? Draw your guess.
flow.kid: Stand one leg in blue water. Stand one in red water. What will the flower look like tomorrow? Draw it.

flow.do: In the morning, look at the flower closely and compare it with the guess.
flow.say: Look! Which side is blue, and which side is red? Did the colours mix?
flow.kid: Look at your flower. Is it purple? Or is one side blue and one side red?

check.q: A white flower's stem was split, and each half stood in a different colour. The flower came out half blue and half red. What does that show?
options: The tubes from each half of the stem go to their own part of the flower
The colours fought and the strongest won
All the water mixes together in the middle of the stem
check.why: Each water tube runs on its own, from the bottom of the stem to one part of the flower. Water in one tube does not mix with water in the tubes beside it. So the blue tubes fed one side and the red tubes fed the other. Picking 'all the water mixes' is a very sensible guess, because the stem looks like one solid thing. The flower shows it is really a bundle of separate tubes.

flow.think: If one root of a big tree is cut, which branches might go thirsty?

activities.context: In this activity you split a white flower's stem into two halves. Each half drinks a different colour. The flower shows which tubes go where.

activities.title: The Water Chain (act it out)

materials.item: a staircase, or a line of cushions on the floor as steps
3 or more people, or soft toys for a child playing alone

activities.safety: Walk slowly on the stairs and hold the railing. Do not pull hard on anyone's arms.

schedule.what: Act out water being pulled up a tube, and a bubble breaking the chain.

activities.record: Draw the chain of water people on the stairs, with the top one floating off as vapour.

flow.do: Everyone stands in a line up the stairs, holding hands. The bottom person is in the soil. The top person is at the leaf hole.
flow.say: We are water molecules inside one tiny tube in a stem. We hold hands, because water sticks to itself. The bottom of the stairs is the root. The top is a leaf.
flow.kid: Stand in a line up the stairs. Hold hands. You are water inside a stem. The top of the stairs is the leaf.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Water Chain. People hold hands up a staircase to act out how water is pulled up a plant.

flow.do: 1. The top person lets go and walks away, waving: they have evaporated into the air. 2. Everyone steps up one stair. 3. A new person, or a toy, joins at the bottom. 4. Repeat a few times.
flow.say: The sun warms the leaf. The top drop evaporates and floats away. Everyone steps up. A new drop comes in at the roots. That's how water climbs!
flow.kid: The top person waves and floats away. Everyone steps up one stair. Someone new joins at the bottom. Again!

good: The one who left at the top.
The sun, by making the top one evaporate.

flow.parent: This is the cohesion-tension idea. Evaporation at the leaf pulls on the whole chain. The chain holds because water molecules cling to each other.

flow.do: Now one person in the middle lets go of hands: they are an air bubble. The top person leaves again. Can the people below the gap step up?
flow.say: Oh no, an air bubble! Someone in the middle let go. Now when the top drop leaves, can the bottom of the chain still be pulled up?
flow.kid: An air bubble! Someone in the middle lets go. Now the top one leaves. Can the bottom of the chain still move up?

check.q: In the Water Chain, someone in the middle let go of hands, like an air bubble. What happens to the people below the gap?
options: They keep stepping up as before
They get stuck, because nothing is pulling them any more
They jump over the gap
check.why: The pull only travels along hands that are held. Below the gap, nothing is pulling. In a real plant, an air bubble in a tube breaks the thread of water. Then that tube stops carrying water. Picking 'keep stepping up' usually means thinking the roots push the water. Roots push only a little.

flow.do: Talk about how a plant copes with bubbles.
flow.say: A plant has thousands of tubes side by side. If one gets a bubble, the water can go round it through the others.
flow.kid: A plant has thousands of tubes. If one gets a bubble, water uses the others.
flow.think: Why do flower sellers cut stems under water? Think about the air bubble person.

activities.context: This is a short play on a staircase. People hold hands to act out water climbing up a tube in a plant, pulled from the top.

setup.caption: 3. Someone lets go: a bubble. The chain below stops.

activities.title: Bring Back the Wilted Coriander

materials.item: a bunch of coriander, palak or mint that has gone floppy
a glass of cool water and a bowl of water
kitchen scissors, used by a grown-up

schedule.what: Revive a wilted bunch, and check after an hour.

activities.record: Draw the bunch before and after. Write how long it took to stand up.

flow.do: Leave a small bunch of coriander out of the fridge for a few hours until it wilts. Feel it with your child.
flow.say: Feel these leaves. They are soft and floppy. Why do you think they have gone like this?
flow.kid: Touch the floppy coriander. Is it soft or crisp? Why do you think it drooped?

good: It lost water.
It has no roots to drink with.
The water left through the leaves.

flow.context: This is the first step of Bring Back the Wilted Coriander. You take a floppy bunch of coriander and help it drink until it stands up again.

flow.do: 1. Hold the stems under water in the bowl. 2. Snip about 1 cm off the bottoms, under the water. 3. Stand the bunch in the glass of cool water straight away.
flow.say: We cut under water, so no air bubbles get into the tubes. Now the leaves can pull water up again.
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up to snip the stems under water. Stand the bunch in a glass of water.

flow.do: After an hour, feel and look at the bunch again. Compare with the drawing.
flow.say: Feel it now. What changed? Where did the stiffness come from?
flow.kid: After one hour, touch it again. Is it crisp now? Where did the water go?

check.q: The wilted coriander stood in water for an hour and became crisp again. Why?
options: Water went up the stems and filled the cells, so they pushed against each other and stood firm
The cold water froze the leaves stiff
The leaves soaked water in from the air
check.why: Each cell has a stretchy bag inside. When water fills the bags, the cells press hard on each other, like water balloons packed in a bag. That makes leaves and stems firm. Picking 'froze stiff' mixes up cool water with ice. Picking 'from the air' misses that the water came up from the glass, through the stems.

flow.do: Talk about how flower and vegetable sellers keep things fresh.
flow.say: Next time we go to the sabzi market, look at how sellers keep greens fresh. Do they sprinkle water? Keep them in the shade? Stand them in buckets?
flow.kid: At the market, look at how sellers keep greens fresh. Water? Shade? Buckets?
flow.think: A plant in soil can wilt at noon and stand up again in the evening. What changes between noon and evening?

activities.context: In this activity you take a bunch of coriander that has gone floppy and help it drink. It shows why plants wilt, and how water makes them firm.

activities.title: Bubbles from a Leaf: find the hidden holes

materials.item: 2 or 3 freshly picked leaves, such as hibiscus, money plant or rose
a glass bowl and warm water from the tap, about as warm as a bath
a magnifying glass
optional: a cheap pocket microscope, clear nail polish and clear sticky tape

activities.safety: A grown-up pours the warm water. Use water as warm as a bath, never boiling. Nail polish is used only by a grown-up, in an airy room.

schedule.what: Watch bubbles come out of a leaf, and look for leaf holes.

activities.record: Draw the leaf, with dots where the bubbles came out. Write which side had more bubbles.

flow.do: 1. Fill the glass bowl with warm water. 2. Push a fresh leaf under the water with a spoon and hold it there. 3. Watch both sides of the leaf closely for a minute or two.
flow.say: Watch the leaf carefully. Do you see tiny bubbles? Which side are they coming from?
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up for warm water in a bowl. Push a leaf under. Watch closely. See tiny bubbles?

ask.q: Where are the bubbles coming from?
good: The underside of the leaf.
Tiny holes in the leaf.

flow.context: This is the first step of Bubbles from a Leaf. You hold a fresh leaf under warm water and watch air bubble out of its tiny holes.

flow.do: 1. Turn the leaf over and compare the two sides. 2. Count the bubbles on each side for one minute.
flow.say: The warm water makes the air inside the leaf swell and come out through the tiny holes. Which side has more holes?
flow.kid: Count the bubbles on each side for one minute. Which side has more?

check.q: A leaf held under warm water gives off tiny bubbles, mostly from its underside. Why?
options: The leaf is breathing out like a fish
Air inside the leaf swells in the warm water and escapes through tiny holes, which are mostly on the underside
The leaf is melting
check.why: A leaf is full of tiny air spaces, joined to the outside by thousands of holes called stomata. Warmth makes the air swell and squeeze out of the holes. Many leaves have most of their holes underneath, out of the hot sun, which helps them lose less water. Picking 'breathing like a fish' is a lovely idea. But these bubbles come from the warm water making the air swell.

flow.do: Optional, with a pocket microscope. 1. A grown-up paints a small patch of clear nail polish on the underside of a leaf. 2. Let it dry for 10 minutes. 3. Press clear sticky tape on it and peel it off. Stick the tape on a glass slide or a clear plastic sheet. 4. Look at it under the microscope.
flow.say: This peel is a copy of the leaf's skin. Can you see little shapes like mouths, or coffee beans? Those are the leaf holes, with their two guard cells.
flow.kid: Look through the microscope. See tiny shapes like mouths? Those are the leaf's holes!
flow.parent: A cheap 60 to 120 times pocket microscope is enough. If you have no microscope, skip this step. A phone camera through a magnifying glass sometimes works too.

activities.context: In this activity you put a fresh leaf in warm water and watch tiny bubbles come out. They show where a leaf's hidden holes are.

activities.title: Climbing Tea and the Great Straw Test

materials.item: a strip of paper towel or tissue, and a cup of tea or coloured water
6 drinking straws, sticky tape, and a glass of water
a ruler

activities.safety: Use cool tea or coloured water, never hot. Do not share straws.

schedule.what: Watch water creep up paper, then test how high you can suck water with joined straws.

activities.record: Write how high the tea climbed up the paper after 10 minutes. Write how many joined straws you could still drink through.

flow.do: 1. Hang a strip of paper towel so its bottom end just dips into a cup of coloured water. 2. Watch for 10 minutes. 3. Measure how high the colour climbs.
flow.say: Watch the water climb up the paper all by itself. It clings to the paper and to itself. That's called capillary action.
flow.kid: Dip the end of a paper strip into coloured water. Watch it climb! Measure how high it goes in 10 minutes.

ask.q: Did it keep climbing for ever?
good: No, it slowed down and stopped.
It only went a few centimetres.

flow.context: This is the first step of Climbing Tea and the Great Straw Test. You watch water creep up paper by itself, and test how high you can suck water through straws.

flow.do: 1. Drink a little water through one straw. 2. Tape two straws end to end, and try again. 3. Keep adding straws, and taping the joins tightly, until it gets very hard.
flow.say: Sucking takes air out of the straw. Then the air outside pushes the water up. Let's see how long a straw you can still drink from.
flow.kid: Drink through one straw. Now tape two straws together and try. Then three. When does it get too hard?
flow.parent: Tape every join well, because leaks of air make it fail early. Most children manage 3 to 5 straws, about a metre. Even a perfect pump could only lift water about 10 metres this way.

flow.do: Compare the paper, the straw and a tall tree.
flow.say: The paper lifted water a few centimetres. The best pump in the world could lift it about 10 metres by sucking. But the tallest tree is about 116 metres tall. So how does a tree do it?
flow.kid: Paper lifts water a little. Sucking lifts it up to 10 metres at most. The tallest tree is 116 metres! How?

check.q: Paper lifts water a few centimetres, and sucking can lift it about 10 metres at most. How does water reach the top of a 116 metre tree?
options: The tree sucks very hard, like a giant straw
The leaves let water evaporate, and that pulls up unbroken threads of water that hold together
The water creeps up like tea up a tissue
check.why: A tree is not a straw. A straw needs air to push the water up, and that can only work up to about 10 metres. Creeping up thin gaps only lifts water a little way. Instead, each tube holds a thread of water that hangs together, and evaporation pulls it up from the top. Picking 'a giant straw' is a natural guess. This test shows why it cannot be the answer.

activities.context: In this activity you watch coloured water creep up a paper strip. Then you test how high you can suck water through joined straws. Both are compared with how a tall tree lifts water.

activities.title: The Dawn Drop Hunt

materials.item: a magnifying glass
a patch of grass, a lawn or a park, early in the morning

activities.safety: Go outside only with a grown-up. Wear chappals on wet grass.

schedule.what: Look for water drops on grass and leaves just after sunrise.

activities.record: Draw a grass blade with a drop at its tip. Draw a leaf covered in tiny dew drops. Write how they are different.

flow.do: Just after sunrise, go to a patch of grass. Look closely at the tips of the grass blades, and at leaves of other small plants.
flow.say: Look at the very tips of the grass blades. Some have one round drop sitting right at the tip. Other leaves are covered all over with tiny drops.
flow.kid: Go out early with a grown-up. Look at grass tips. Is there one drop right at the end? Or tiny drops all over?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Dawn Drop Hunt. Early in the morning, you look for two kinds of water drops on grass and leaves.

flow.do: Explain the two kinds of drops.
flow.say: Tiny drops all over a leaf are usually dew. Water vapour in the cool night air turned back into drops on the cold leaf. But one big drop right at the tip came from inside the plant. The roots pushed water up in the night, and it was squeezed out of special holes at the tip.
flow.kid: Tiny drops all over are dew, from the air. One drop at the tip came from inside the plant! The roots pushed it out.

check.q: On the Dawn Drop Hunt, you find one round drop sitting right at the tip of a grass blade. Where did it most likely come from?
options: From inside the plant, pushed up by the roots in the night
From a cloud
From an insect
check.why: At night the leaf holes are mostly closed, so little water leaves as vapour. But roots can keep pushing water up a little. The water is squeezed out of tiny openings at the leaf tip. Scientists call this guttation. Dew is different: it forms from the air, as tiny drops all over a surface. Picking 'from a cloud' mixes it up with rain.

flow.do: Come back after an hour of sun and look again.
flow.say: Where have the drops gone? Into the air? Back into the leaf?
flow.kid: Come back in an hour. Where did the drops go?
flow.think: At night the roots push. In the day the leaves pull. Which do you think is stronger?

activities.context: This is an early-morning hunt for water drops on grass. You learn to tell two kinds of drops apart. Dew comes from the air. Other drops are pushed out of the leaf tips by the plant.

projects.title: Be Stephen Hales: weigh a plant's thirst

materials.item: a small potted plant, such as tulsi, coleus or a chilli plant
a kitchen weighing scale that shows grams
a plastic bag or cling film, and a rubber band
a notebook and a pencil

projects.safety: Lift the pot carefully with both hands. Cover only the soil and pot, never the leaves.

schedule.what: Water the plant, seal the pot and soil in plastic, and weigh it.
Weigh it at the same time. Write the weather.
Weigh it at the same time. Write the weather.
Weigh it at the same time. Write the weather.
Weigh it, work out how much water it lost each day, draw a bar chart, then water the plant and uncover it.

projects.record: A table of the weight each day, the weather each day, and the grams lost since the day before. Then a bar chart of grams lost each day.

flow.do: 1. Water the plant well and let it drain for an hour. 2. Wrap the pot and the soil in a plastic bag. Tie it round the base of the stem, so only the leaves are open to the air. 3. Weigh the whole thing and write it down.
flow.say: Almost 300 years ago, Stephen Hales did this with a sunflower. We've covered the soil, so water can only escape through the leaves. If the plant gets lighter, the lost weight is water that went out of the leaves.
flow.kid: Water the plant. Wrap the pot and soil in plastic. Leave the leaves open. Weigh it. Write the number.
flow.context: This is the first step of Be Stephen Hales. You weigh a potted plant every day to find out how much water it lets out through its leaves.

flow.do: 1. Each day, at the same time, weigh the plant. 2. Write the weight and the weather: sunny, cloudy, rainy or windy.
flow.say: Same time every day, so it's fair. How many grams lighter is it today? Was it a sunny day?
flow.kid: Weigh the plant at the same time each day. Write the number and the weather.
flow.parent: One gram of weight lost is about one millilitre of water, a fifth of a teaspoon. A small plant may lose 10 to 50 grams a day, more on hot dry days.

flow.do: 1. On day 5, weigh it once more. 2. Work out the grams lost each day by taking each day's weight away from the day before. 3. Draw a bar for each day.
flow.say: Yesterday it weighed this much, today this much. Take one from the other to find what it lost. Which day did it lose the most? What was the weather?
flow.kid: Take today's weight away from yesterday's. That is the water it let out. Draw a bar for each day.

check.q: In the Be Stephen Hales project, the plant weighed 512 grams on Monday and 480 grams on Tuesday. How much water did it let out?
options: 32 grams
992 grams
480 grams
check.why: The weight lost is the difference. 512 take away 480 is 32. So it let out about 32 grams of water, which is about 32 millilitres. Picking 992 means adding the two weights instead of finding the difference.

chart.title: Made-up example: water a tulsi plant let out each day
chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what results can look like. Your numbers will be different.

flow.do: 1. Look at the bar chart and the weather together. 2. Then water the plant and take the plastic off.
flow.say: Which weather made the plant let out the most water? Why do you think that is?
flow.kid: Look at your bars. Which day was tallest? What was the weather that day?

ask.q: Why did it lose more on sunny or windy days?
good: Water evaporates faster in sun and wind.
The leaves open their holes more in the sun.

flow.think: If this small plant lets out this much, how much does a big neem tree let out?

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Let's finish like real scientists. Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Finish like a scientist. Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: plants let out more water on sunny, windy days. What I saw: my tulsi lost 38 grams on the windy day and only 8 grams on the rainy day. Why: wind and sun make water evaporate from the leaves faster, and damp air slows it down.

challenges.title: Lift the Water
challenges.problem: Move coloured water from a low cup up into a higher empty cup, without pouring, pumping or sucking. Plants lift water without any of those. Can you?
constraints: You cannot pick up the low cup or pour from it.
No sucking, squeezing, spoons or syringes.
Use only things from home, like paper, cloth, string and sponge.
materials: 2 cups or glasses, one standing on a stack of books so it is higher
paper towel, cotton cloth, thick cotton string, a sponge, tissue, chalk
general: A strip of paper towel or cotton cloth from the low cup up and over into the high cup. The water creeps up by capillary action and drips down the other side.
Thick cotton string or a twisted strip of cloth, which works like a wick in a diya.
creative: Make the high cup only a little higher, and the wick short. Capillary action only lifts water a few centimetres.
Wet the wick first, so the water thread is already unbroken. That is like cutting stems under water.
Try a wick with leaves: stand a leafy stem in the low cup and catch the water it lets out in a bag. A plant is the best water lifter of all.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own water lifter. Draw it, try it, and measure how much water reached the high cup in 24 hours.

flow.do: 1. Put one cup on a stack of books, and an empty cup beside it on the table. 2. Fill the low cup with coloured water. Leave the high cup empty.
flow.say: Here's the challenge. Get water from this low cup up into the high cup, with no pouring and no sucking. A plant does it every day.
flow.kid: Fill the low cup with coloured water. Put the empty cup up high. Get the water up there, with no pouring!
flow.parent: Put the full cup low and the empty cup high, on books. This makes it a real lift, not just a siphon downhill.
flow.context: This is the first step of Lift the Water. You must get coloured water from a low cup up into a high cup without pouring or sucking.

flow.do: Before trying, draw or write three ideas together.
flow.say: Engineers plan first. What have you seen that makes water climb by itself?
flow.kid: Plan first, like an engineer. Draw three ideas. What makes water climb by itself?

flow.do: 1. Try each idea. 2. Leave the best one overnight. 3. In the morning, measure the water in the high cup with a spoon.
flow.say: Let's try your ideas. Which one is moving the most water? Let's leave it overnight.
flow.kid: Try each idea. Which works best? Leave it overnight. Measure in the morning.

check.q: In Lift the Water, a strip of paper towel lifts coloured water a few centimetres into a cup. What is lifting the water?
options: Magic in the paper
Capillary action: water clinging to the paper fibres and to itself
Gravity pulling it up
check.why: Water sticks to the paper's tiny fibres and to itself, so it creeps up the thin gaps. This is capillary action. Gravity pulls water down, not up, which is why the wick only works for small heights. Plants use capillary action a little, but mostly they pull water up by evaporation.

flow.do: Read the usual solutions and the creative ideas. Then invent your own.
flow.say: Here is what most people try, and some creative ideas. Can you beat them?
flow.kid: Read the usual ideas and the creative ones. Now invent your own. Can you beat them?
flow.think: Clay pots and cotton wicks have been used to water plants slowly for hundreds of years. Why might farmers want water to move slowly?

challenges.context: This is an engineering challenge. You must lift coloured water from a low cup into a high cup. You can only use the tricks that plants and wicks use.

challenges.title: The Holiday Plant Sitter
challenges.problem: Your family is going away for a week. Design a way to keep a potted plant watered, with nobody at home.
constraints: It must not flood the plant, because roots need air too.
It must cost almost nothing, using things from home.
materials: thick cotton string or a strip of old cotton cloth
a small unglazed clay pot or diya
a clear plastic bag or a large clear bottle
general: A wick: one end of a cotton string in a bottle of water, the other end pushed into the soil. Water creeps along it into the soil.
An upside-down bottle with small holes in its cap, pushed into the soil, letting water out slowly.
A clear bag or cut bottle over the whole plant like a tent, so the water it lets out stays inside and drips back.
creative: A small unglazed clay pot buried in the soil and filled with water. Water seeps out through the clay. Farmers in many dry places, including parts of India, have watered plants like this for a very long time.
Move the plant into the shade and out of the wind while you are away, so it lets out less water.
Group several pots close together so they keep the air around them damp.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own plant sitter. Draw it, test it for 3 days before the holiday, and weigh the pot each day to see if it is keeping the soil damp.

flow.do: Look at the plant together and talk about how it loses water.
flow.say: This plant lets water out of its leaves every day, and drinks from the soil. If nobody waters it for a week, what happens?
flow.kid: This plant loses water from its leaves every day. What happens if nobody waters it for a week?
flow.context: This is the first step of The Holiday Plant Sitter. You design a way to keep a potted plant watered for a week with nobody home.

flow.do: Draw three designs. For each one, ask: does it bring water in, or stop water leaving?
flow.say: There are two ways to help. Bring water in slowly. Or stop so much leaving. Which do your designs do?
flow.kid: Draw three designs. Does each one bring water in? Or stop water leaving?

check.q: In the Holiday Plant Sitter, you put a clear bag over the whole plant like a tent. How does that help?
options: It keeps the plant warm
The air inside gets damp, so less water leaves the leaves, and what does leave drips back down
It stops the plant from making food
check.why: Leaves lose water fastest into dry, moving air. Inside a bag, the air fills with water vapour and stays still. So the leaves lose much less, and the drops that form run back into the soil. Picking 'keeps it warm' is partly true, which is why the plant must stay out of hot sun while covered.

flow.do: 1. Build your best design. 2. Weigh the pot. 3. Test it for 3 days, weighing the pot each day.
flow.say: If the pot stays about the same weight, water is coming in as fast as it goes out. If it gets much lighter, the plant is drying.
flow.kid: Build your best design. Weigh the pot each day for 3 days. Is it staying heavy?
flow.parent: Keep the plant out of direct sun if it is under a bag, or it may overheat. Make sure the pot has a drainage hole so a leaky bottle cannot drown the roots.

flow.do: Compare your design with the usual and creative ideas, and improve it.
flow.say: Which idea kept the soil damp best? What would you change?
flow.kid: Did your design keep the soil damp? What would make it even better?
flow.think: A forest keeps its own air damp, because all the trees let out water together. Is a forest a bit like a giant plant sitter?

quiz.p: Which part of a plant soaks up most of its water?
quiz.why: Roots, and their root hairs, soak up water from the soil. Picking 'leaves' usually comes from watering plants from above. Leaves mostly let water out.

quiz.p: Water climbs up a stem through…
quiz.why: Xylem tubes run from the roots to the leaves. Picking 'air spaces' mixes up the tubes with the air spaces inside a leaf.

quiz.p: In the Blue Climb, why do we also stand one flower in plain water?
opts: To compare, so we know the colour came from the water
quiz.context: In the Blue Climb experiment, you stand a white flower or a celery stalk in coloured water. Then you watch where the colour goes.
quiz.why: The plain-water flower stays white. That shows the colour in the other flower came from the coloured water, not from the flower itself. Picking 'thirsty' misses the point of a comparison.

quiz.p: After the Blue Climb, a cut celery stalk shows coloured dots. They are…
quiz.context: In the Blue Climb experiment, you stand a white flower or a celery stalk in coloured water. Then you watch where the colour goes.
quiz.why: The dots are bundles of xylem tubes that the coloured water climbed up. Picking 'spots of paint' means thinking the colour just sits anywhere in the stem.

opts: Water leaving the leaves as vapour
quiz.why: Transpiration is water leaving the leaves as invisible vapour. Picking 'leaves making food' mixes it up with photosynthesis, a different job of the leaf.

quiz.p: What mostly pulls water up a tall tree?
quiz.why: As water evaporates from the leaves, it pulls the threads of water up the tubes. Roots push only a little, and trees have no heart. Picking 'a pump in the roots' is an old idea that cannot explain tall trees.

quiz.p: In the Leafy or Bare test, which stem drank more?
quiz.context: In the Leafy or Bare test, two stems stand in two bottles of water with oil on top. One stem has leaves and one has none. You measure how far each water level drops.
quiz.why: The leaves let water out into the air, which pulls more water up. Picking 'the bare stem' usually means thinking a stem with no leaves must be thirstier.

opts: It loses water faster than it can take it in
quiz.why: When water leaves faster than it comes in, the cells go soft and the plant droops. Too much water can also harm roots. But that is not what usually makes a plant droop on a hot day.

quiz.p: Why do flower sellers cut stems again under water?
opts: To stop air bubbles blocking the water tubes
To make the flowers smell nice
quiz.why: An air bubble breaks the thread of water in a tube. Cutting under water keeps air out. Picking 'clean the knife' misses that the water is for the stem.

quiz.p: In the Leafy or Bare test, the leafy stem's water dropped 18 mm and the bare stem's 3 mm. How many millimetres more did the leafy stem drink?
quiz.context: In the Leafy or Bare test, two stems stand in two bottles of water with oil on top. One stem has leaves and one has none. You measure how far each water level drops.
quiz.why: 18 take away 3 is 15. So the leafy stem drank 15 mm more. Picking 6 means dividing, which tells you how many times as much, not how many more.

quiz.p: In the Sweating Branch test, what should be different between the two branches?
opts: The kind of plant and the bag
quiz.context: In the Sweating Branch test, you tie clear bags over two leafy branches. One is in the sun and one is in the shade. The bags catch the water the leaves let out.
quiz.why: In a fair test, you change only one thing. Then you know that thing caused the difference. Picking 'the kind of plant and the bag' means two changes, so you could not tell which one mattered.

quiz.p: Jagadish Chandra Bose thought living cells pump water up stems. What do most scientists think today?
opts: Water is pulled up from the top by evaporation, so Bose was wrong about this
quiz.why: The pulling idea of Dixon and Joly is accepted today. Bose was wrong about this one idea, but he made many other great discoveries. Picking 'nobody has any idea' is not fair to the evidence. Scientists are sure about the main idea, though some details are still being studied.

quiz.p: Which of these do scientists still NOT know for sure?
opts: Exactly how tall a tree could ever grow
That water travels up the stem
quiz.why: Scientists agree water travels up stems and leaves let it out. But the limit on tree height is still argued about. Estimates say about 122 to 130 metres for redwoods.

quiz.p: Why does a thread of water not snap when it is pulled up a tree?
opts: Water molecules hold on to each other
quiz.why: Water molecules pull on each other with tiny electric pulls. This is called cohesion. Picking 'the tree glues it' is a good image, but the 'glue' is in the water itself.

quiz.p: Where does the energy to lift water up a tree come from?
quiz.why: Sunlight makes water evaporate from the leaves, and that does the pulling. The tree does not spend its own food energy to lift water. Picking 'the soil' mixes up where the water comes from with what lifts it.

applications: Flower sellers and florists cut stems under water and keep them in buckets, so cut flowers keep drinking.
Coloured flowers for weddings and festivals are often made by standing white flowers in coloured water.
Farmers water in the early morning or evening, when less water escapes into the air.
Drip irrigation sends water straight to the roots, so less is wasted.
Buried clay pots and cotton wicks water plants slowly in dry places.
Gardeners trim some leaves off a plant when they move it, so it loses less water while its roots settle.
Greenhouses and plastic tunnels keep the air damp, so young plants lose less water.
Trees planted along streets cool cities, partly by letting water evaporate from their leaves.
Forests protect rain. Keeping forests standing helps keep rain falling on farms further away.
Weather forecasters and climate scientists include water from plants in their models of rain.
Scientists measure the sap flow in trees with tiny heat sensors, to see how thirsty a forest is.
Farmers and scientists breed crops that close their leaf holes sooner, to survive dry spells.
Astronauts grow food on the space station using wicks, because water does not drip down in space.
Wood is made of old water tubes. Its grain, which carpenters follow when they cut, is the lines of those tubes.
Sugarcane juice and coconut water are stored water and sugar, carried in by the plant's tubes.

open_questions.q: How do trees fix their water tubes after an air bubble blocks them?
open_questions.why_open: Some studies suggest plants can refill blocked tubes, even while the water is under tension. Others think the measurements were fooled by the way the stems were cut. Scientists still argue.

open_questions.q: How tall could a tree ever grow?
open_questions.why_open: Water sets one limit, estimated at about 122 to 130 metres for redwoods. Wind, weight and getting food to the top may set others. Nobody can test it by waiting a thousand years.

open_questions.q: Does anything listen to the clicks of thirsty plants?
open_questions.why_open: The clicks were recorded in 2023. Whether moths, mice or other plants use them is unknown.

open_questions.q: Exactly how much of the rain over land comes from water that plants send up?
open_questions.why_open: Different ways of measuring give answers from about 60 to 90 out of every 100 drops rising from land.

open_questions.q: How does a plant decide when to close its leaf holes?
open_questions.why_open: Signals come from the leaves, the roots and the water in the tubes. How a plant weighs them all together is still being studied.

open_questions.q: Do living cells next to the water tubes help the water move, as Bose once thought, even a little?
open_questions.why_open: The main pull is from the leaves. But living cells next to the tubes may help refill them or steer water, and that is still being studied.

open_questions.q: How did the very first water tubes evolve in plants, more than 400 million years ago?
open_questions.why_open: Early fossils are tiny and rare. New finds keep changing the story.

open_questions.q: How will hotter, drier weather change the world's forests?
open_questions.why_open: In droughts, trees can get so many air bubbles in their tubes that they die. Scientists are trying to predict which forests are most at risk.

maths.problem: In the Blue Climb, the colour climbed 3 cm up a balsam stem in the first hour. If it kept climbing at the same speed, how high would it be after 4 hours? Look at the line chart.
maths.explain: Each hour adds 3 cm. After 4 hours that is 4 lots of 3 cm. 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 12, or 4 × 3 = 12. So the colour would be 12 cm up the stem. Real stems may speed up or slow down, which is why we measure instead of only working it out.
maths.context: In the Blue Climb experiment, you stand a balsam stem in coloured water. Balsam stems are see-through, so you can watch the colour climb and measure it with a ruler.

chart.title: Made-up example: how high the colour climbed up a balsam stem

maths.why_maths: Measuring once tells you where the water is. Multiplying tells you where it is heading, and the next check tells you if your guess was right.

maths.problem: In the Leafy or Bare test, the leafy stem's water was at 95 mm on the ruler at the start. Two days later it was at 77 mm. The bare stem's went from 95 mm to 92 mm. How much did each one drop? How much more did the leafy stem drink?
maths.answer: The leafy stem's water dropped 18 mm and the bare stem's 3 mm. The leafy stem drank 15 mm more.
maths.explain: For the leafy stem, 95 take away 77 is 18 mm. For the bare stem, 95 take away 92 is 3 mm. Then 18 take away 3 is 15. So the leafy stem drank 15 mm more of water. 18 divided by 3 is 6, so it drank 6 times as much.
maths.context: In the Leafy or Bare test, two stems stand in two identical bottles of water with oil on top. One stem has leaves and one has none. You mark the water levels and measure how far they drop.

answer_chart.title: How much the water level dropped in 2 days

maths.why_maths: A water level on its own means little. Taking the end from the start tells you how much the plant actually drank. Comparing the two stems tells you how much the leaves matter.

maths.problem: Look at the ruler in the picture. It measures the water level in the Leafy or Bare bottle. The big numbers are centimetres. The small marks between them are millimetres. What is the reading, in millimetres?
maths.answer: 77 millimetres, which is 7 centimetres and 7 millimetres.
maths.explain: The water is past the 7 cm mark, and 7 small marks further on. Each centimetre has 10 millimetres, so 7 cm is 70 mm. 70 + 7 = 77 mm.
maths.context: In the Leafy or Bare test, you hold a ruler next to a bottle. You read where the water level is. The tiny marks are millimetres. Ten of them make one centimetre.

chart.title: A ruler beside the bottle, in centimetres
chart.label: Each small mark is 1 millimetre.

maths.why_maths: The water level only moves a few millimetres a day. Reading the small marks on a ruler is what lets you see a plant drinking.

maths.problem: In Be Stephen Hales, a plant was weighed each day. It weighed 512 g on Monday, 480 g on Tuesday, 466 g on Wednesday and 428 g on Thursday. How much water did it let out each day? Draw a bar chart. Which day did it lose the most?
maths.answer: 32 g, then 14 g, then 38 g. It lost the most from Wednesday to Thursday.
maths.explain: Take each day's weight from the day before. 512 take away 480 is 32. 480 take away 466 is 14. 466 take away 428 is 38. Draw a bar for each. The tallest bar, 38 g, is Wednesday to Thursday. In the made-up example, that was the windy day.
maths.context: In the Be Stephen Hales project, you wrap a pot's soil in plastic. Then water can only leave through the leaves. You weigh the plant at the same time every day. The weight it loses is water it let out.

answer_chart.title: Water the plant let out each day (grams)

maths.why_maths: A list of weights hides the story. Subtracting shows how much the plant drank each day. A bar chart then lets you match the tallest bar to the weather.

maths.problem: A big tree lets out about 200 litres of water on a hot day. A bucket holds 10 litres. How many buckets is that? How many buckets in one week of hot days?
maths.answer: 20 buckets in a day, and 140 buckets in a week.
maths.explain: 200 divided by 10 is 20, so 20 buckets in a day. A week has 7 days. 20 × 7 = 140. So 140 buckets in a week, all lifted by the Sun, with no pump and no heart.
maths.context: In the Sweating Branch test, one small branch gave off a spoon or two of water in two hours. A whole big tree has thousands of branches, all day long. 200 litres is a rough example for a big tree on a hot day.

answer_chart.title: Buckets of water a big tree lifts on hot days (200 litres a day, 10 litres a bucket)

maths.why_maths: Hundreds of litres is hard to picture. Turning it into buckets you could carry shows how much work the Sun does in one tree.

roots.context: We have been following one drop of water from a plant's root to its leaf, and into the air. Now we ask what that journey tells us about ourselves and the world.

three.who_am_i: The water in your body was once in clouds, rivers and trees.
three.what_is_life: A tree has no heart. The Sun's warmth lifts its water.
three.what_is_this_world: The same water has gone round the world for billions of years.

roots.thread: One drop of water climbs a tree, leaves as vapour, becomes a cloud and falls as rain. Then it climbs another tree, or flows into you. DeepKids believes this is the One moving through many shapes. The drop is never really separate. It is always part of one great water, passing through.

teachings.teaching: Rivers flow east and west and reach the sea. In the sea, no river can say, 'I am this river.' They are all the sea.
teachings.link: The water in a leaf, a cloud and your glass is one water, moving on. It never stays one drop for long.

teachings.teaching: The best way is like water. Water helps all living things and does not fight. It flows to low places others avoid.
teachings.link: Water climbs every plant quietly, giving life, then lets go into the air.

teachings.teaching: Listen to the reed flute. It was cut from the reed bed, and now it sings of wanting to return.
teachings.link: A reed is a hollow stem, like the tubes that carry water up a plant. Its song is air and emptiness.

science.text: Water is pulled up a plant from the top. It sticks to itself like a chain of hands. As it leaves the leaves, it pulls more up behind it.
How the tallest trees stop their water chains from snapping is still being worked out.

other_view.view: The Buddha taught that nothing has a fixed, lasting self. Many Buddhists would say there is no great water underneath, only changing drops, moment by moment.

practice.title: Follow one sip
practice.say: Let's pour a little water into a steel tumbler. Hold it and look at it for a moment. Now take one slow sip. Close your eyes and feel it go down. Breathe slowly. Where was this water before? A cloud? A river? A mango tree? Where will it go next?
practice.kid: Take one slow sip of water. Close your eyes. Feel it go down. Where was this water before?

ask: Who does water really belong to?
A plant lets almost all its water go. Is letting go always a loss?
Is a drop of rain still itself when it reaches the sea?
roots.art: One water drop drawn on a loop from root to leaf to cloud to rain to a child's glass, around a tall banyan tree.
